speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 7, the debate on the motion of the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 54, to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers.

Mr. Speaker, in proceeding further with the discussion of Bill No. 54, I would like to refer briefly to what would appear to be a studied campaign which has been carried on in various parts of Canada during the past few weeks to discredit the provisions of the bill. Almost invariably hon. members who have discussed this measure from the opposition benches have, in respect to claims and contentions made, found refuge in that campaign of, I think, entire, but I hope not deliberate, misrepresentation. I want to refer to some of the statements that have been made in that connection. Here is one coming 
from the jurisdiction of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) which says:
The Criminal Code of Canada, in one of its sections, has penalties which fit the crimes, known as trusts, mergers and combines, whenever these are in restraint of trade, and does it in a much simpler way than the Premier's bill, as well as providing heavy penalties. It should be sufficient for the purposes without the enactment of legislation that will handicap trade and make burdensome interference with the conduct of private business. The great objection to his bill is that it is wholly inquisitorial, and that "any person resident in Canada of the full age of twenty-one who is of opinion that a combine exists, or is being formed," may start an investigation which, on mere suspicion will subject business men to no end of trouble and expense.
There is a wholesome truth in the old saying that a half truth is worse than a falsehood. Then, we come to another one from the jurisdiction of my hon. friend for London (Mr. White), which says:
One curious clause makes it illegal to fix a resale price.
It is not true, but it gets over in an editorial just the same.
In other words, a manufacturing firm which does a national business and advertises from end to end of Canada its products at one price could not fix this price.
Nothing in the bill suggests the accuracy of that statement, unless it could be conclusively shown that the fixing of that price was a detriment to the public, to the consumer, to the producer. Then, this same article pays me a compliment by saying:
That bold trust-buster, Hon. James Murdock, the Minister of Labour, has machinery he needs now if he will only make use of it.
An absolutely unqualified misstatement of fact, as every hon. member familiar with the legislation which has for some time been on our statute books, knows. Yet that kind of bunk gets over from the Opposition press, and, may I say without disrespect, is parroted by hon. gentlemen from the Opposition benches.
Then, we have another one. Listen to this: It comes from not very far distant:
The process, too, is simple, the laying of an information before a competent magistrate puts the accused on their defence, creates the opportunity for bringing out the facts, and if there has been guilt, provides adequate punishment. The government bill is' of a type that appeals to those who confound fuss with efficiency and noise with progress.
That listens very nicely, to the uninitiated, but it does not fool any hon. member or any other citizen of Canada? Who ever dreamed for a moment of the feasibility of his approaching some magistrate and suggesting that there was a combine detrimental to him or to other consumers or producers, and then

Combines-Mr. Murdock
getting proper redress at the hands of the court? All hon. gentlemen know how far he would get. One thing these editorials and various others that might be quoted overlook is the fact that the provisions of the criminal code dealing with combines have been useless since the days when my right hon. friend and his colleagues took good care to make the Combines Investigation Act moribund and of no effect. It has been impossible, therefore, to use the provisions of the criminal code, section 498, in dealing with the most dreaded or contemptible combine that might exist in Canada.
Would the minister care to state from which papers those editorials were taken?
British Columbian, New Westminster, B.C., London Free Fress and the Montreal Gazette.
What are their politics?

If my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) will pardon two or three additional references to the statements which he made in his speech on this subject I should like to deal first with this. The hon. gentleman said:
Now I turn to what is my chief criticism of the bill, that in effect it declares to be a crime that which is, without question ordinary, sound business sense.
With my hon. friend I agree and am ready to assume that condition prevails so far as the great majority of combinations existent in Canada to-day are concerned, and I am ready to charitably assume that many of those combinations are not combines carrying on their operations to the detriment of the public whether consumeis or producers, but I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that Professor Alfred Marshall, the leading economist in the world, stated in Principles of Economics at page 447:
But perhaps the public show too much indulgence to those who argue that a trade combination or a trust is the only means available for securing reasonable steadiness of prices.
Then my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre went on to argue at considerable length as to what might happen to certain dairy industries, and I want to remind him of some of his previous views in that regard. The exact statement of the hon. gentleman was:
It was shown beyond all peradventure that the Ottawa Dairy, while a distinct monopoly under this clause, did operate in the interest of the public.
Let us read the record to see what was the trend of the hon. gentleman's mind when
that particular inquiry was being made. At page 304 of the examination of Alderman W. Guertin, before the Special Committee on the High Cost of Living, I find this:
By Mr. Devlin.
Q. Do you know anything about the Producers' Milk Company?-A. Yes, they endeavoured to lower the price of milk in Ottawa.
Q. When did they go into business?-A. About 7 or 8 months ago.
Q. This spring?-A. Not this spring, 7 or 8 months ago. That would be last year.
Q. Had the fact of their going into business and putting teams in the streets delivering milk the effect of reducing the price?-A. We found that the fact of their going into competition was reducing the cost of milk. The manager was telling me that they were going-
Q. We will not mind hearsay evidence, but from your own personal examination by how many cents was there a drop in milk?-A. There was a drop, through competition of two cents-three cents I should say because the Ottawa Dairy started by lowering to 11 cent3, then the Producers retaliated by lowering to 10 cents, then it was lowered to 10 cents.
Q. What is it now?-A. 10 cents.
Mr. Stevens: You are a mighty lucky city. It is fifteen or sixteen cents elsewhere.
Which would almost convey to the uninitiated or casual reader that there was an expression of regret in the hon. gentleman s language that the traffic was not being made to carry all that it would bear.
I desire now to make some further references to the speech of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. One of his statements was:
Everything is here which is going to pile harass-ments, vexation and expense on legitimate business: that is all in the measure,-investigation after investigation, circle after circle, but never any goal.
That was the summing up of the right hon. gentleman in regard to this particular measure. Then he goes further and reviews anti-combine legislation, and states that in 1888 parliament first sought to enact anti-combine legislation and apppointed a committee to work out some effective measure. I assume that that is justification for believing that the right hon. gentleman conceives that there has been as far back as 1888 the necessity for dealing with combines detrimental to the public interest. I happen to have in my hand a copy of the budget speech of 1878, and I find printed as an appendix to that budget speech some illuminating evidence as to conditions in those years gone by, indicating that there was even at that time marked necessity on this North American continent to deal with combines detrimental to the public interest. This appendix refers to an extract from the message delivered by the Governor of the state of New York to the legislature of that state at Albany in 1878. I read a portion cf it to show just what it is
Combines-Mr. Murdock

the public has been complaining of, and what it is believed this particular Bill No. 54, will to a very substantial extent protect the public from. After noting one of the causes of the currency inflation in the States the governor went on to say:
At the same time, another great evil was strongly developed; individuals and corporations engaged in various branches of manufacture, taking advantage of the necessities of the government, rushed to congress, and by every means in their power procured for their own benefit the levy of what we call protective duties under the false pretence of raising revenue for the government, but really to compel consumers to pay exorbitant prices for the favoured article thus protected.
So that was regarded in 1878 as being the underlying cause of certain combinations detrimental to the public interest. Then my right hon. friend inquires, in a manner such as no other member of the House could inquire What is this sacred sanctimonious principle?" and he was very properly advised by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy) that what is proposed is a square deal to everyone in this country. I am willing, however, to let my hon. friend (Mr. Healy) take the responsibility of answering that question of the leader of the Opposition, but I shall quote the right hon. gentleman's own words before he became a right honourable. We find that on July 4, 1919, the Combines and Fair Prices Act was before this parliament. Let me quote from Hansard what happened on that occasion:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Meighen, Bill No. 167, concerning the Investigation and Restraint of Combines, Monopolies, Trusts and Mergers, and the Withholding and Enhancement of the Price of Commodities, was read the second time, and the House went into eommittee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the chair.
On clause 2-definitions. "Combine":
Mr. McKenzie: Perhaps the work of the committee might be abbreviated by the minister stating wherein this bill differs from the old Combines Act or is it practically the same?
< ^ my hon. friends to follow me closely in this quotation to ascertain where some things came from.
Mr. Meighen: No, it is very different. I think, however, the committee already has a pretty full idea of the intent and scope of this measure from the discussion in a previous act. I direct the attention of the committee to the clause:
The expression "combine" is used in this act with intended relation to articles of commerce, and it shall be deemed to have reference only to such combines, immediately hereinafter defined, as, with relation as aforesaid, have, in the opinion of the Board of Commerce of Canada (or of a single member thereof acting under authority of and for the purposes of section eight of this act) operated, or are likely to operate, to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, consumers, producers or others and, limited as aforesaid, the said expression as used in this act shall be deemed to include,-
(a) mergers trusts and monopolies, so called.
TMr. Murdock.]
That is to say, the scope of the operations of this board as affecting combines shall be directed against such combines as are detrimental to the public interest. In other words, this act recognizes the fact that there may be combines, and there may be purposes of combines, that are in full accord with the public interest, in the interest of the country. For example, combinations of capital, and combinations for the purpose of working together towards increasing export trade The greater our export trade the better to the country, that is a good, laudable practice and a good reason for amalgamation, because there are times when it can be better secured, indeed almost always, by that means. But if that same combination operates for the purpose of keeping down the wages of its employees, combines for that purpose, or for the purpose of putting up the cost to its consumers, above what is reasonable to those purchasers that is detrimental to the interests of the public, and for so doing a combine comes within the operations of the act and is answerable to this board.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that is fairly good Liberal doctrine and is sufficient to justify the proposal to incorporate practically the same definitions of a combine detrimental to the public interest as are found in the proposed bill No. 54, now before the House. My right hon. friend also states as his opinion, that the Privy Council's judgment really does not assail or impugn part one of the Combines and Fair Prices Act which is now on the statutes books of Canada. In that statement I>
as f layman, concur and I think my friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) would also concur. But I want to make some inquiries. If that is so why has it been possible for the people of Canada to be denied the protection accorded by part one of the Combines and Fair Prices Act during all of the later months of the late government's regime? Why was not something done to continue the protection or to appoint some tribunal that would take care of the combines detrimental to the public interest that might exist? We find my right hon. friend on June 29, 1920. twelve days before he had reached the goal of his very commendable ambition to become the Prime Minister of Canada, making this statement in regard to the Board of Commerce :
Why in the first place, there is a law conferring certain powers and imposing certain duties on a board, a law written and planted on the statute books, known to the board when they took office, a law with the operation of which nobody can interefere, a law which they have the courts of the land at their disposal to enforce.
Mv right hon. friend, of course, did not intend to make a statement that was incorrect but the statement contained in the quotation which I have given is absolutely incorrect, as I propose and undertake to prove. This was the 29th of June, 1920, and no one knows better than my right hon. friend that the Board of Commerce had been a wooden gun, so far as protecting the interest of the consumers,

Combines-Mr. Murdock
the public, and others against unfair combines, for more than four months prior to that particular day. No one could know that fact any better than my right hon. friend, and yet we find him getting up in parliament and making the statement referred to. The reason for that fact is, that four months prior to that date the chairman of the Board of Commerce had resigned-to be exact on the 23rd day of February, 1920-had resigned hurriedly, and from that very moment the Board of Commerce, to the extent of protecting the public against combines detrimental to it, ceased to function under the language of the law. In other words, prosecutions could not be instituted without a chief commissioner. The law has been so framed, whether unintentionally or purposely I do not know. The latter part of subsection 2 of section 9 of the Combines Investigation Act says:
In the case of an investigation ordered the chief commissioner shall fix the time and place for such investigation, of which the secretary shall notify in writing the applicant or his authorized counsel.
And so as the weary weeks and months had gone by-four long months-without the board being permitted to do anything or get anywhere in relation to the things for which presumably it was paid, we find the right hon. gentleman on the 29th June rising in the House-as he also did last night-expressing surprise and inquiring wherein the board had been interfered with by absolute prevention on the part of certain honourable gentlemen, or by failing to place the board in a position to do things which the Combines and Fair Prices Act, in part one, provided should be done in the interests of the public. My right hon. friend, capable legal gentleman he is, should be very familiar with that fact.
I am sorry I am not. Will the minister tell us what we failed to do that the act called on us to do?
The right hon. gentleman failed to do anything that the act called on him to do. That is only another very delightful way which my right hon. friend has of dodging the real point.

I do not know what the issue is. The minister says they could not do anything because they were prevented, and to show that they were prevented he says that the minister would not do what he should have done in order to enable the board to act. I want him to tell me what it was. I do not know. I want him to establish what he says and show that it was our duty to do it.

The act, of course, as the right hon. member would try to convey, does
not provide that immediately on the chief commissionership becoming vacant, if the board is to proceed to function in the interests of the public as by law intended, a chief commissioner shall be appointed, but the language of the act was so fearfully and wonderfully prepared, either inadvertently or intentionally, that that was the net result, and that fact was called to the attention of hon. members at that time sitting on the treasury benches of paliament, not once but repeatedly.

The failure then was to appoint a chief commissioner to succeed Judge Robson. That is what I understand. Does the minister say that, in the absence of Judge Robson, or upon his resignation, the commission as it existed then had not power to act?
Exactly, Mr. Speaker.
He says what is wrong.

The claim that is made- and I am sure my right hon. friend is aware of this, and if not he can get unlimited legal advice to that effect-is that in a more important aspect of the intended functioning of the board, that board was powerless to proceed without a chief commissioner.
Not at all. That is not the fact. Although the minister, with all his talents, was on the board, the board was just as powerless before as after the resignation.
It was a board of the right hon. member's creation.
The minister was not.

There is considerable in what the right hon. member says, that the board was practically as useless before the resignation as aftewards. Again, I am not informed as to whether this was inadvertently or intentionally done.

Will the hon. member not admit that it was an act of the board committed or performed after the resignation of Judge Robson, that was called in question before the courts, and that the courts in their judgment in no way even referred to the absence of the chief commissioner as affecting the validity of the act? It was just as vaild after as before. It was the hon. member that was wrong-not the act.

My right hon. friend is a little off in his dates and in his facts. He overlooked the fact, that the cause of the resignation was the writing of a letter which, in some way, came to be sent by other members of the staff in connection with a case that was being prepared for the courts.
Combines-Mr. Murdock
I did not mention anything about that.
Order, order.
Order.

In other words, it is not correct to state that it was after the resignation of the chairman that facts in connection with the appeal case were prepared and sent forward. It is true there was a completed case, and the courts were ready to go ahead and deal with the case that had been prepared for submission to them.

The minister missed my point. Was it not an act or an order of the board issued after the resignation of Judge Robson that was brought before the courts on appeal, and did the courts not decide it without even referring to the absence or nonexistence of a chief commissioner?-showing that the board had perfect power to act after as well as before.

My right hon. friend is aware that there were two cases submitted, the latter case being by consent of the parties for the purpose of testing the validity of the act, for the purpose of clearing up and trying to get somewhere, and to give the government what they appeared to want, and that was the assurance that the Board of Commerce had no right to function in the interests of the public in protecting the public against combines, monopolies and mergers. That is, by every act, what appeared to be the desire of the government.
What act?
Every act and omission to act.
Name one of them. The hon member is deceiving nobody by this evasion, except perhaps himself.

I will call my right hon. friend s attention to certain actions of his government, indicating their particular intent in regard to certain of these matters. In addition to the presumed and intended duties of members of the Board of Commerce, in the latter part of January, or, to be exact, on the 19th day of January, 1920, the members of the board were hurriedly called to the office of the Minister of the Interior, who desired to convey to them the understanding that they were to be appointed to some additional and new duties. They were to be Paper Controllers for the Dominion of Canada, as the result of the resignation, or pending resignation, I forget which, of the then Paper Con-
troller. What were the facts in connection with this paper control? A price of $80 a ton on newsprint paper had been fixed and continued in effect as applicable to various newspaper concerns all over Canada, when at that particular time, or during a part of that time, the spot market price for newsprint was from S90 to as high as $165 a ton, determined by how hard up some newspaper was to secure the product to get out its issue. As a result of this condition, the switches of the Fort Frances Pulp and Paper Mill had been spiked down, and an ultimatum had been served on the Backus company that no more would they be permitted to ship paper across the international boundary until they complied with the language and intent of the Paper Controller's orders. So that was the situation on the nineteenth day of January when we were hurriedly called to the office of the Minister of the Interior to be invested with our new functions and authority.
Who was he?

The Minister of the Interior at that time was the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). On two occasions on that 19t,h day of January we were called to interview the right hon. gentleman and also the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice, and then in the evening the intimation was given "Nothing doing just now". That very night, or early the next morning, a trusted and capable civil servant was despatched to Fort Frances, with the result that within a few short days, the spikes were taken out of the switches, and the Fort Frances Pulp and Paper Company were permitted to send their paper unhindered across the international boundary. The civil servant returned to Ottawa, and gentlemen connected with the then government indicated, by their talk and scowling looks and suggested actions, that they were very seriously concerned about the unfortunate act and disobedience of the civil servant who had gone to Fort Frances to do exactly what he was told to do. Then on the 30th day of January we were again called in and were made full-fleged paper controllers. At the suggestion of and under a Privy Council order prepared by the then Minister of the Interior, we started to carry on that additional farce of fixing a price for newsprint paper to the newspaper companies of Canada at about one-half the price that the market called for. Yet on that particular day would there not have been great clamour and dissent throughout Canada, as there was in certain cases, when it was proposed to fix the price of milk to babies or bread to hungry

Combines-Mr. Murdock
people? No, that must not be done; that would be earned by this government across the seas; carried to the Supreme Court of Canada first, where three eminent judges sitting on the Supreme Court benches decided that the contested rights were satisfactory, and by law contemplated and as the Board of Commerce had contended. All a part of the beautiful farce of fooling the public.
Mr! MEIGHEN: Will the hon. gentleman permit me? I have tried to get out-
I still have the floor.

I am aware of that. That is about all the hon. member has. I have tried to extract out of this mass of verbiage something attributable to the government. All I have got is this: He states that the commissioner who went west prior to the appointment of the Board of Commerce as paper controller, was instructed to do what he did by the then government. That commissioner was Mr. Breadner. I tell my hon. friend that Mr. Breadner had no such instructions, and my hon. friend cannot produce a statement of Mr. Breadner that he had.

My right hon. friend can, of course, put what construction he likes on what I say. I stated and I repeat that, selfevidently and without any question, what was done at Fort Frances was what was intended to be done. I say that even in disregard of the attempt of certain hon. gentlemen to fool the Board of Commerce later into the belief that nothing of the kind was intended.
I tell the hon. gentlemap that I had to do with the matter-
Order.

I deny the right, Mr. Speaker-I want to know-Has this hon. gentleman or any hon. gentleman the right to speak of the intentions of men with whom he did not come into contact, whose word he cannot bring in support of his statement, and against the statement of one who actually had to do with the matter? Such conduct is not only infamous; it is of a character I cannot describe in this House.

I understand the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) rises to a question of privilege. No hon. member in the debates can impute motives, and I would ask that the debate be continued, but without motives being imputed to any hon. member.
I gladly withdraw if the right hon. member considers that I was in any way imputing improper motives to him.
I would much rather that he would make what he says good.

The right hon. member last night and again to-day was particularly anxious about making good. He seems to have overlooked entirely what so many thousands of the people of Canada have known for many months, or since the sixth of December, 1921, that the case has been tried and the verdict rendered in regard to the alleged and camouflaged pretence by the late government of providing a Combines and Fair Prices Act for the protection of the consumers, producers and others. The verdict of the people of Canada has been rendered on that subject, and my right hon. friend is very safe in showing bravado now, three years late, in having something investigated, and judgment passed upon it, that all the people of Canada passed judgment on about sixteen months ago.
I want to refer now as fast as possible to two or three other matters in connection with Bill 54, as proposed. The right hon. member last evening stated:
In so far as this legislation makes something a crime which is defined here-I refer to clause 26-it is at least very doubtful to my mind if that clause is within our constitutional powers.
My right hon. friend and the other hon. members who are behind him, seem to take great objection to this particular new "crime" to be incorporated in the statutes of Canada:
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $10,000 or to two yars' imprisonment, or if a corporation to a penalty not exceeding $25,000, who is a party or privy to or knowingly assists in the formation or operation of a combine as defined in this act.
My right hon. friend and those associated with him, as well as certain newspapers in Canada, appear to be much concerned as to whether that particular crime and the penalty therefor can be made effective. If the right hon. gentleman would only look at the legislation which he proposed and upheld some three years ago he would find that it was very much more drastic in its intent than what is now proposed. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, he stated last night that the first part of the Combines and Fair Prices Act of 1919 had not in his judgment been changed by the Privy Council decision, Further, he said:
But X venture to say again the Criminal Code provisions will be more practically useful left alone. Improve them if you will; make them wider if you will; but leave them as Criminal Code provisions. Do not provide for any investigation.
That is exactly what my right hon. friend and his associates appear to be afraid of-
Combines-Mr. Munlock

an investigation in regard to some particular concern.

I did not say that. If the hon. gentleman will read the rest of it he will find that, either in that sentence or in one further on, I state that it is worthless to provide for an investigation unless the investigators are given power to give effect to their findings.

Very well. It can at least be noted that the right hon. gentleman rallies promptly to the support of some combine, monopoly or price fixing arrangement that is detrimental to consumers, producers and others. That is the first thought. And he argues, as only he can argue, to show why the re-affirming of section 498 of the Criminal Code would be satisfactory and would give all the relief that is possible or necessary. Now, I just want to refer to a statement made by my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) last evening. That hon. gentleman, it seems to me, was very discourteous to, and inconsiderate of, the rights of citizens of Canada, particularly those who might happen to be section men, firemen, brakemen-men employed in logging operations and others engaged in similar occupations. Listen to the position taken by the hon. gentleman; just see how he classes these people. He refers to "six uninformed, irresponsible individuals" asking for an investigation.
Just a moment. Will the hon. gentleman read the preceding explanatory sentence in which I distinctly stated that 1 was not saying ignorant persons, but persons uninformed as to facts.

My hon. friend in tiie preceding sentence does say:
I do not say ignorant people, but uninformed people, are very prone io complain of businesses or institutions wherever they may be. Six uninformed, irresponsible individuals may ask for an investigation.
Well, I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that the right to ask for such an investigation was conceded to these "uninformed," "irresponsible" and "ignorant" persons by his government in 1919 when passing through this House the Combines and Fair Prices Act. I do not see therefore why "six individuals" can now be classed as irresponsible and ignorant just because it is proposed to give under Bill 54 the same rights that were contemplated in that act. Now, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion-
Hear, hear.
Do not do that now, because I may not stop.
I think they want you to go on.

My right hon. friend and others have made a reference to the alleged numerous investigations that are to be conducted before arriving at a starting point in Bill 54. Let me briefly analyze this proposition so that we may ascertain whether or not that is just the case. The leader of the opposition, as I recall, indicated that any individual could, under section 498 of the Criminal Code, reaffirmed, go to a magistrate and lay an affirmation against some combine, trust monopoly or merger, secure the necessary investigation, and drag that combine, trust, monopoly or merger into court. He actually says a thing of that kind
4 p.m. and expects, I presume, that the hon. members of this House will believe it. My right hon. friend knows, as does every other hon. gentleman sitting behind him, that almost assuredly, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, if an individual undertook to lay information as to the existence of any combine or trust or monopoly or merger, he would not have had the necessary access to the facts that would permit him to make that affirmation in detail sufficiently to ensure the issuance of a warrant or the bringing into court of the alleged combine or whatever it might be. My right hon. friend knows that.

My hon. friend knows - it does not take a lawyer to know it-that you do not need to allege any fact whatever save this, that you have reason to believe and do believe that the illegal combine, or whatever it might be, exists. If that is done, then, unless there is sufficient reason to the contrary, the attorney general will take the matter over and conduct the prosecution.

And my right hon. friend would know, of a surety, that there would possibly be, as he suggested by his qualifying remark, a sufficient reason to the contrary.
Mr.. MEIGHEN: That would be the fault of the attorney general.

Wherever the fault would be, it would be a wooden gun; it would be a thing unavailable to the section man, to the logger, to the small merchant; they could not grapple with anything so large. But entitle these same individuals to some reasonable inquiry to ascertain if the suspicions they hold are well founded, and the result is different. So

Combines-Mr. Murdock
this Bill No. 54 permits six individuals to send in a statement of their belief, giving all the facts as they know them. The registrar of the boards of investigation, without any publicity-at least without the publicity that would result should action be taken under the Criminal Code-inquires, presumably by correspondence, or otherwise as he sees proper, into the facts, with a view to ascertaining whether the claims made by the six individuals are well founded.

Will my hon. friend permit a question? If it is true that- it is impossible to get action under the Criminal Code, how was it that under section 498 there were at least six prosecutions, while under the Combines Investigation Act of 1910 there was only one inquiry, the case of the United Shoe Company, and no prosecution?
I would be m a better position to answer my hon. friend if he would tell me when these six prosecu irons under the Criminal Code took place.

I will do so. Rex vs Elliott, 1904; Rex vs Master Plumbers, 1905; Rex vs Gage, 1907; Rex vs Clark, 1907; Rex vs Beckett et al, 1907; Rex vs McMichael, 1907; Rex vs Day, 1905. Then there were several later civil actions in connection with which the provisions of the Criminal Code regarding combines were the deciding factor. Included in the cases were Hatley vs Elliott, 1903; Wampole and Company vs Kam Company, Limited, 1906; Weidmarm vs Schragg, 1912; and there were several others. The first seven cases I mentioned were under the Criminal Code, section 498, whereas, as I have pointed out, under the Combines Act there was only the case of the United Shoe Company- an investigation, but no prosecution.

My hon. friend is entirely correct about the number of prosecutions proceeded with under the Combines Act of 1910; that has not been questioned. As to the prosecutions under the Criminal Code, it would be interesting, if my hon friend and I had time to do so, to indicate to the House just what were the proceedings. For instance, in the case of Rex vs Beckett, 1907, my recollection is that a decision was handed down some eight or nine years later. In any case, if I am not mistaken, it took a great length of time to deal with it, and then the results were practically nil. But is it not reasonable to assume that the plan now proposed is a better one-that of having an inquiry made on the basis presumably, of the good judgment of the registrar? And my assumption is that
a peculiarly qualified person should be chosen to fill that position. The registrar would make the necessary preliminary investigation, and if there appeared to be something requiring further attention he would so report to the minister. The minister would no doubt communicate with the Governor in Council, and if it was so decided they would appoint a commissioner for the particular purpose of investigating the alleged combine, monopoly, trust or merger. The commissioner would not, as has been suggested, simply ramble round at his sweet will here and there and everywhere, inquiring into this, that, or the other thing; he would be a man particularly fitted to make that specific inquiry. If after the commissioner had made his investigation it was found that a (rust, combine, monopoly or merger existed detumental to the interests of the public, then the matter would be taken up in a court of competent jurisdiction and if guilt was established the penalty would be imposed.
I want to say just this in conclusion. My right hon. friend has stated:
Let me repeat: All this legislation is simply running in a circle. It is another circle you have to go round; it is just another stump round which you can chase the flat-footed fiend of monopoly.
How different from the language used by the right hon. gentleman in 1919 when the Combines and Fair Prices Act was being proposed. Then he talked as if he were desirous of protecting the public against unfair combinations, but now he and certain of his associates who have spoken would wish to make it appear that there is the same camouflage in this bill as was characteristic of the Combines and Fair Prices Act. I assure hon. members of this House that if I thought there was any such camouflage in the provisions of this bill as were developed and worked out under the Combines and Fair Prices Act, the creature of my right hon. friend's government, I would oppose the measure with every means at my command. If that weie the case I should not be here to claim that by this bill it is proposed to give the plain people of Canada an opportunity to secure redress where there may be in effect combines, monopolies, trusts or mergers detrimental to the public interest.

I
do not intend to follow the hon. gentleman (Mr. Murdock) who has just sat down except to disagree somewhat with the position he has taken, because he is here to-day as the defender of a proposal dealing with combines which has been introduced by the Prime Minister of Canada, which has been endorsed by his gov-



Combines-Mr. Maclean (York)
eminent and endorsed by his party, notwithstanding a number of dissentients from his own followers, for last night there was a kind of backfire from his own side of the House. But he is attempting to deal with the question of the regulation of combines and trusts in this country, and he is approaching it in the conventional way-going by the old formula, and the old formula is no good at this time. It is true that the measure before the House now has all the .marks of being ponti-ficial. It is a law passed by parliament, and you must obey it; if you do not, look our for yourself. Perhaps!
We have had legislation of that kind in this House for a great many years; the different acts have all been enumerated. Now as an old member of the House and one who has read something in the past, who has studied this question as best he could from his own point of view, I want to give my experience and to suggest a new formula for approaching a situation of this kind. We have a formula now on the statute books, and we have a formula in the past in the records of previous statesmen in this country. They have a very fine phrase in French, which is very significant. They speak of L'Action Catholique or catholic action, L'Action Agricole or farmers' action or the farmers' kick, something that has punch to it. And the punch must come not so much from the act of parliament as from action by the government of the country, who are responsible for the conduct of public affairs and for the relief of grievances that may happen to come before parliament and are in the mouths of the people every day. I mean by direct action on the part of the government.
I am speaking for six hundred thousand women who are to vote in the next election in this country, and a good many of them are to vote in my own province in a few weeks. I am going to say that the greatest combine in Canada to-day is the sugar trust in Montreal, and it is not to be approached and the grievance is not to be remedied by legislation exactly of this kind, although I am going to vote for this measure because all my life I have advocated the regulation of combines and trusts. I am going to do so mainly for this reason, that an opportunity is being given in parliament to-day by the introduction of this bill to direct the attention of the people to these combines and to the necessity of their removal.
Now what is the thing to do in connection with the sugar trust? I do not exactly say, do what Sir John A. Macdonald did in the past but it has been done in parliament, and to-day there is this big sugar combine in Canada and the women of this country are be-

ginning to organize against it, and they will be heard from within a few weeks. The duty of the government to-day in connection with that sugar combine is to exercise the powers conferred on them as a government. The Minister of Finance is coming down to this House on Friday with his budget proposals and his revision of the tariff. Now what I would suggest-and I make this suggestion to the Prime Minister and his party and to the government-is that their immediate duty in dealing with this sugar combine is to send a straight and short message to the sugar combine in Montreal: If you do not by Friday afford relief to the housekeepers and every citizen of this country who uses sugar, by a reduction of the price, there will be a reduction in the duty on sugar.
Hear, hear.

That is practical politics. That is dealing with combines in the way they ought to be dealt with, and that is the only way to deal with them. I have seen these matters brought up in the courts for forty years. I have seen it as a young man, as a member of this House, as a newspaper man. I have seen it and I know where action of that kind always ends. But what you want is a strong man in office. A strong Prime Minister and a strong government in office, with a strong party behind them, who will regulate these trusts and send these short telegrams to these men saying: If you do not have the price changed by Friday, look out! The way to put the fear of God into these men is by direct action of that kind.
Just to give the House an illustration of what a combine is, we have what is thought to be by a great many people a banking combine in Canada. I met an old friend of mine the other dajq and he made a reference to the Merchants' Bank and what occurred in connection with it. He said, "Mr. Maclean, if my old friend Mr. Courtney-at one time Deputy Minister of Finance-had been there when the disclosures were made about the Merchants' Bank he would have had the bank directors and president here in Ottawa in ten hours and said to them: If you do not correct this abuse and stop this waste of the funds of the bank, as it should have been stopped, immediate action will be taken." There would then have been a different story in regard to the Merchants' Bank. Action is not in courts: action is in the government and is the thing necessary. The action is in the Prime Minister. The action is in his party, and the action in regard to combines

Combines-Mr. Madeem (York)
to-day is to intimate to these men: If there is no relief in the price of sugar by Friday, look out!
I will go a step further. If the sugar combine does not pay attention to the women housekeepers of Canada, and half a million of them are going to vote in the next election, if it does not pay attention to this condition of affairs I would have the Minister of Finance wire to two great banks, the Royal Bank with headquarters at Montreal, one whose president is Sir Herbert Holt, and to the Bank of Nova Scotia with headquarters in Toronto, and I would tell these banks who are behind the sugar combine that if relief is not afforded to the housekeepers and the people of this country, men, women and children, for everyone uses sugar, and a high price is being put on it, then we as the government of Canada will not give you the facilities we are giving you now for rediscount. Provide the money yourselves for the sugar trust. If that did not have the desired effect I would send another telegram to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I know a good deal about them. I have been more or less a friend of theirs in the past. I believe in protection in this country, but I do not believe in the extortion of trusts. I would send a wire to the Manufacturers' Association and I would say: If this thing is not regulated by the sugar trust, and is not to be regulated by the banks that are behind the sugar trust, we are going to revise the tariff on some other things. The next organizations to be dealt with should be the combines that control textiles, enamelled ware, and other commodities of domestic use. It is no good to say, "We will send you to the courts. We are geing to appoint a registrar to hold hearings in private"-as some gentlemen want; and the same thing applies if held in public-"to inquire into the grievances of the public." The government should say, "We are going to find out what are the grievances of the public. We are Liberals and we consider it to be our duty to afford relief to the people. We are to get the public that relief and we are about to get it in a quick way."
Now, as to the sugar combine I want to say something else. That sugar combine wrecked more Canadian capitalists who put their money into the securities of the sugar trust than almost any other organization I know of; and I think if the leader of the government were to ask some of his old colleagues who had experience of the sugar trust they would tell him some surprising things. The situation, however, resolves itself into this-that relief lies more in action on the
164i
part of the government than in making laws and appointing judges, sending for the constable and hauling men into court. The great thing is for the government to send out an order that within so many hours this thing, which is very unfair to the public, must end. They are coming to that in other countries. In the United States Mr. Hoover is trying to deal with these questions, and in some respects he is getting relief. Previous presidents of the United States, including Mr. Taft, and their attorney generals, have dealt with this matter and have found that the only effective way to deal with these people is to summon them to Washington or to Ottawa and say "You must do so and so. You may show me if I am wrong and if you do so the government will listen to you. If you cannot, the public are entitled to get relief and we will see that they get it through action on our part in regard to the tariff." Mr. Harding is probably going to take some action along this line when he starts his campaign for the next presidential election in the course of two or three weeks.
Now let me take up another point. It is all very well to say that we will apply the law. The government are making some progress under previous legislation that we had but it was not effective. That is the great thing, it was not effective, and it dicl not deal with the situation but had the matter referred to the courts. Why, in the great court case of Jarndyce vs. Jarndvce, of which Dickens tells us, how many years did it take to get a verdict? There is a quick method of settling public grievances to-day and it does not lie so much in legislation as in action on the part of the government in power. In short, my contention is that this legislation will not be as efficacious as action on the part of the government if they choose to exercise the power. It is up to them to take action and it is up to the public to make its wishes known when there is an election if the government do not take that action. We must remember that there has been a great addition to the voting power of the country now that women are entitled to vote. The woman has arrived in politics, she is in this House, and she is out in public life to exercise her vote. It is all very well for newspapers to show their regard for women by instructing them in matters of fashion and dress; and giving details of the wedding of the Duke and Duchess of York and the presents received by the royal pair. The real question to the women of this country is housekeeping, and sugar is one of the great items that enters into the question. A sugar trust exists in this country. We are about to revise the

Mr. Maclean (York)
tariff, on Friday next, and I ask what action will the government take on the protest of the 600,000 women throughout Canada who now have votes?
There is a combine-so the farmers tell us-indeed evidence has been given before a parliamentary committee to that effect- in shipping in this country. That combine has treated the farmers infamously in regard to freight rates. Well, it does not need any legislation to regulate the actions of that combine. They now enjoy rights in connection with the canals. Those waterways are owned by the people and they should refuse the shipping trust the use of our canals. Or the government could order the directors of the National railways, which now belong to the people, to reduce rates and thus serve the interest of the public as against the shipping trust. It is not necessary to do that by legislation; it could be done by the government. Action on the part of the government is the effective way to do it. As to the shipping trust I am going to tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways something; there is a suspicion in the minds of a great many people that the National Railways are a party to this shipping trust. That ought to be investigated. If that be the case, Sir Henry Thornton has probably come into it by inheritance. If it is the case that there is an understanding between the National Railways and the shipping trust by which shipping rates are maintained, it ought to be made possible for the farmers to ship their grain by railway. Now, the regulation of all this does not lie in legislation. As I have already said it lies in action on the part of the government in controlling and regulating the use of the canals and, at some points, the harbour dues. In a hundred different ways a combine can be reached by the power that is vested in the government when the public are treated unfairly.
Now, as to the alleged combination of the banks: They are up now for legislation, and we also have the question of securing credit for the farmers of Canada which apparently they need. It may be true that that relief is not to come by way of money advanced by the banks, but by way of the creation of new organizations-loan banks as they are called in the United States-or in other ways. It is up to the government to see that practical legislation is enacted along this line and not leave this matter so much to the banks.
I want to give the Prime Minister credit for what he is doing here to-day; he is approaching the question in the legislation that he has brought down. But there is something

that follows from that action on his part. Does he know that if he does not make good
in these matters he is simply preparing a rod for his own back? That is the point the Prime Minister should bear in mind; he will be judged by what he does, and most of all by what he does in connection with the sugar combine. I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is not here. I would like to impress my views upon him, but he will hear of them sooner or later. And the sugar combine will read to-morrow what I have said and they may be shaking in their shoes. I would like to know what that great newspaper the Montreal Star will have to say when it reads that a proposal was made in parliament to give relief to the housewives of Canada from these enormous sugar charges.
I have tried to present the real issue and to show what is to be done. There are many combines. I confess that I am a protectionist and I am glad that Canada has built up her industries by a system of protection. But these industries must be square with the people who give them privileges, and with parliament which passes the legislation that concerns the welfare of the country. There has been great profiteering. There never was such an era of profiteering, some of it under government regulations, as we have witnessed during and since the war. The war is not altogether responsible for present conditions. The profiteering which has taken place since the war has had a most far-reaching effect, and is going to stay with us, not only through our lives, but through the lives of our children, and we are not going to recover until we get down to hard facts and wherever we find a wrong, to right it, and to compel reparations, which is the phrase used now in connection with the war. That will be accomplished by the efficiency, the power, the study and the determination of the government of the day. So far as the present act is an attempt to follow previous legislation, I will give the government credit for it, but let them remember that they are on trial now. It is not the sugar trust that is on trial at the present time so much as it is the government which has introduced this legislation. If it affords some relief the government will get credit for it in the country. The people want relief to-day from the shipping combine, and in the regulation of our national railways, if these are a party in any sense to the shipping combine, and in the regulation of the other trusts and combines which exist in the country. In common with other hon. members of the House, I have been flooded with appeals from the druggists and

Combines-Mr. Forke
other combinations. They have presented a special appeal containing very scientific terms. They are saying "Do not deal with our combine." But parliament has to deal with these combines, and is to-day trying to deal with them. The government has introduced something which is not the real remedy, and i am urging to-day that the real formula for dealing with the trust is by direct action by the government, and that action lies through the tariff. We are going to have the tariff resolutions on Friday and will have a debate next week. We will then hear from the women, and I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will listen in on the wires and see whether he is with the women of this country and is going to fight their battles against the sugar and other trusts, because there are many trusts in this country. These trusts are growing and becoming more insolent and defiant every day. I will tell the House what they are doing, as I see it every day in the committees. The danger in this country is i' creating a bloc made of members of the two parties against the national ownership of the railways and against any legislation for the regulation of combines in this country. People ask why should we have three parties in this country when previously we only had two? But you see three parties coming, and they are going to be here for some time. Some people think we are to get rid of them, but parliamentary government is progressing and not going backward. New things turn up. I never was so surprised as when I read in an English newspaper what was going on over there, and read the arguments presented by the best papers in England about the regulation of combines and the building combines that exist. I do not refer to the daily press but to the weekly press.
I am going to close with a reference to a matter which is rather apropos of the present situation. There never was a more sensational week in the history of the New York exchange than last week. Many small investors were closed out; tens of millions of money embarked in stock speculations were lost and will never come back. Queer actions occurred on the stock exchange yesterday, and other things have happened concurrently with the doings on the New York stock exchange. Wheat fell 5 cents a bushel and cotton fell to a much greater extent. The Standard Oil Company has seen fit to reduce the price of gasoline; but sugar goes up, because there is combine in sugar, and there is not a combine in wheat or in cotton. Wherever there has been a combine, or wherever a parliamentary group can be organized irrespective
of parties in parliament to protect these combines, it is being done. I do not know what the outcome of those incidents in the New York stock exchange of last week will be. I am afraid there is a great financial crisis ahead of us. It may be arriving now, and we have an opportunity to-day, in dealing with the tariff, to compel the combines which have used that tariff to deal unfairly with the people of Canada, to right these wrongs. On behalf of the people of Canada I draw the attention of the government to the new formula, and the only practical formula for dealing with combines at this time; that is by direct action on the part of the government, and by telling these combines that if they do not give relief they will be forced to do it by tariff withdrawals. They must not depend on the tariff of this country; the steamship companies must not depend on the use of the canals in the country, and the banking group must not depend on the discounting power of the government in connection with re-discounting. They must be told that only those who treat the people fairly in the matter of combinations will have the favour of the government and of the party in power. As I have always been a protectionist and a friend of the manufacturers, I think the statement may well come from me that the only way to bring these men to time in Canada and in the United States is by the exercise of the power vested in the government and in parliament by way of legislation. But there is a still more efficacious way, and that is by the formula which I have laid before the House, namely that of direct action.

I was a little astonished last evening in listening to the very mild arguments that were presented in favour of this bill by hon. members from the other side of the House. In fact, I can ' almost say that some of them condemned it by the same phrase.
I wish to refer to remarks made by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean).
I am very pleased indeed to listen to some of the advice and the recommendations that he has made to the right hon. Prime Minister. I hope the Prime Minister will listen to the advice given him, more especially when the hon. member called attention to the fact that a deputation of the women of this country was going to call upon him. If hon. members will notice, the subject under discussion by the hon. member for South York was a very sweet one, and consequently worthy of very great attention. I listened with a great deal of pleasure to the speech made by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Combines-Mr. Forke

Evans) last evening. I notice a considerable resemblance between the speech of the free trader and that of the protectionist, when they begin to deal with the subject of combines. The only difference I noticed between the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) and the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), is the fact that one would cut off the dog's tail by inches, and the other would take it right off at the root. I have hopes that as days go by, my hon. friend from South York will find a warm reception over in this corner of the House. I do not think we are very far apart. He consoles himself every now and then by repeating that he is a friend of the manufacturers and he is in favour of protection.
I am in favour of industries prospering in this country.

We in this part of the House can repeat the formula with a little change. We are in favour of just as much free trade as is possible in Canada, and we are also in favour of the manufacturers so after all I do not think there is a great deal of difference between us.
Last night I heard some discussion as to who the people of Canada were and during that discussion there came into my mind an old phrase which, perhaps, most hon. members have heard. The people generally mean the class of people in whom we are particularly interested. We are all fond of talking about "the people," and perhaps some of us have heard of the tailors of Toole street, who put at the top of their paper "We, the people of England." So I imagine some of us view things along pretty much the same lines. We are all in favour of doing what we believe to be in the interest of the people, only we have different points of view, and it makes a great ' deal of difference from what angle we view any subject which is under our consideration. I do not think any of us have anything to say against combinations as such. We believe we are living in a day when people are getting together to work for their mutual advantage. At the same time I have no sympathy with the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), when he says that he believes these combinations are only moving toward a time when we shall have what might be called socialism, when it will be one great combine and that will be the state. There is in the Anglo-Saxon nature something that will always prevent such a combination, because deeply embedded in our nature is the feeling that we always want to have something which we can call our own. I do not care how much a person may prove, in theory, the bene-

ficial effects of socialism, it will never find a resting place among the Anglo-Saxon people.
A few words were said last night as regards newspaper monopoly. Perhaps this is one of the most dangerous monopolies that we can possibly have in a civilized country. We are sometimes inclined to criticize, to find fault with the press; but we cannot possibly do without it; it is the only means of information which we have. I can think of circumstances away back on the prairies, where the people living on their farms have only one source of information and that is the daily paper coming to their homes each evening. They do not know aything about what is occurring anywhere in our Dominion, or in the world, excepting through that paper. How important therefore, it is that we should have news of the best description, news that is accurate, reliable and trustworthy. It is so long sinee I have looked over the Progressive platform, that I have almost forgotten some of the planks contained in it; but I am quite safe because I know they were founded on good and sound principles, and I am pretty nearly sure to come along the beaten path with regard to that. I know there was a plank at the time-and I think it is there yet-that in every newspaper there should be some sort of statement as to who controls its policy and who owns the stock. If we had that information, we could sometimes read between lines and form an accurate judgment as to the reliability of the information contained in a newspaper.
I notice many speakers, whenever they have anything to say about monopolies or combinations, always refer to the wheat board and the attempt that the farmers in the West made to get a monopoly in the selling of wheat. I have given up all hope of ever enlightening some hon. friends as to exactly what that meant, because I do not think we shall ever be able to do so after the months that have passed and the many speeches and explanations that have been made. I will only repeat again that any attempt that was made was simply a matter of stabilizing the price during the season, so that all should reap an equal advantage. I do not think anyone ever thought for a moment that the wheat board would add one cent to the price of wheat in England; the idea was that it would stabilize the price over the different months of the year.
In connection with the bill at present under discussion, I believe it is a move in the right direction. I do not think it will altogether accomplish the ends intended just as long as we have a protective tariff. I know it is usually the custom, when speaking

Combines-Mr. McMaster
of hon. members from this part of the House, to make out that we are out-and-out free traders. I want to make this explanation at this particular time. While I believe free trade is the right principle, we must remember that we are up against, not a treaty, not a theory but a circumstance in this country at the present time, and consequently it is necessary that we should have some revenue. Therefore, so long as the tariff is a means of getting revenue, perhaps we have not so much criticism to oiler in these days as we might have under other conditions.
I want to say a few words in connection with some combinations that have been working in restraint of the agricultural communities. Not very long ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) a question in connection with the shipment of cattle. We know there has already been an investigation as regards ocean rates, and we are perfectly satisfied and convinced that a combination exists there to take the last cent possible out of shipments of cattle. One of the difficulties we have to meet in agriculture at the present time is the loss of morale amongst the agricultural people. I know they are carrying a heavy load of indebtedness upon their shoulders; but at the same time farmers, as a class, are optimists and, as a rule, they look hopefully toward the future, believing that "man never is, but always to be blest." But at present there is a certain lack of morale from the very fact that no matter what may be their exertions, no matter what crops they may raise, the practical outcome will be the same. I speak from experience. I have raised big crops and small crops; but I have always found at the end of the year's transactions, that matters have been so manipulated that only a bare living has been left to the man who has produced the wealth. That is why we want to get to the bottom of combinations in restraint of trade or for the purpose of taking undue advantage of the privileges they have acquired. I have no doubt that all members of this House are anxious for the prosperity and welfare of this Dominion; but at this particular time I would make a plea for the common people, the working people, who after all are just as essential for the welfare of Canada as are our business classes. Every now and then when any attempt is made to adjust any difficulties, we hear this cry: "It will disturb business." Business, apparently, is regarded as something sacred and holy that you must not interfere with. When I think of the hundreds and thousands of men and women scattered throughout this country who are making their living by daily toil, I
am not so tremendously afraid of business; business can take care of itself.
I do not intend to take up any more of the time of the House at present. I will support the bill because I believe it is a move in the right direction. I do not for a moment believe it is going to cure all the evils that exist at the present time. I believe those can be cured only when trade shall flow freely backward and forward in all directions. One of the evils to-day is not the tariff alone. Some people think we look upon the tariff as the cause of all the evils that have overtaken agriculture in these days. The tariff is infinitesimal in comparison with the evils that result from it. In itself it would not be so obnoxious, but it makes possible the very things we are trying to get at and to cure with the present bill. I believe therefore that this is an attempt in the right direction. While it will not cure the whole evil it will at least help to do so, and I am inclined to give it my support. I listened with interest to the very able criticism of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). I am always pleased to follow the criticisms of that right hon. gentleman and I admire his ability, his industry and his energy. In this case, however, I think his criticism was peculiarly weak and lacking in power or conviction. Possibly I have said enough.

A sad but imperative duty compelled me to miss the very interesting debate that took place yesterday, but I have listened attentively to what has been said to-day and have endeavoured to acquaint myself somewhat with the progress of the debate which occupied the attention of the House yesterday. This bill seems to me to be a step in the right direction. I do not propose to discuss it in detail; I think that a great deal of the discussion which took place yesterday might very properly have been reserved until the bill is in committee, when hon. members on both sides of the House will have an opportunity of offering those suggestions which they think fit for the perfecting of the machinery of this legislation. It seems to me that on the second reading of the bill we should discuss its spiijt and essence. Is there a need for such legislation as we have before us this afternoon?
Yes.

That there is such a
need all parties in the House are agreed. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) while he was one of the foremost members of the administration which preceded the present government, placed on the statute books legis-
Combines-Mr. McM aster

lation not dissimilar in character. I do not intend here to enter into any acrimonious discussion as to whether that legislation was right or wrong, whether it was well-conceived or ill-conceived, or whether it functioned to the benefit or to the prejudice of the people. The point I wish to make is this, that in the opinion of the Conservative party of that day, called at that time the Unionist party, it was necessary to have such legislation. Any of us who have examined the industrial and economic structure of our country as it exists at this time are all, I am sure, absolutely convinced that the economic and industrial life of Canada is honeycombed with combines and rings of all sorts. I do not think there is any possibility of dispute so far as that is concerned. It has been said that all combines are not bad. That may be true. There may be that rara avis in our economic life, the beneficent combine, the gathering together of manufacturers or middlemen for the purpose of reducing costs of production or of distribution and of giving the benefit of that reduction to the consumer. I would gladly welcome the acquaintanceship of such a combine, and in the words of the president of the Privy Council of years gone by I would desire to give my tribute of praise to any such institution. When I see such a combination as that I shall not be chary in the expression of my appreciation. But I am afraid that a calm and cool survey of the situation will bring most of us to the unbiassed conclusion that as a rule combines are not made for the purpose of reducing prices but of maintaining or raising them. There is therefore obviously some necessity for somebody to control combines. There is only one objection which in theory is perhaps a sound objection to legislation of this kind, and that is that it interferes with the freedom which should characterize human endeavour; and if we lived in this country under a system by means of which trade could flow freely into and beyond our boundaries, then I would hesitate before giving approval to legislation of this sort. But we cannot get immediately that "consummation devoutly to be wished," and while we maintain to any substantial degree the pro-, tective principle we have to protect the consumers of the country against the exactions of those people who take advantage of the tariff wall in order, in a circumscribed and comparatively narrow market, to charge all that traffic will bear, to the deriment of the consumer. I think that is the sound answer to the otherwise perhaps sound objection 
against such legislation as this, that it interferes with people conducting their own business in their own way. That being the case, I think we are pretty well all agreed as to the necessity for the legislation.
I have little to reply to in the remarks made by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) and the leader of the third
5 p.m. party in the House (Mr. Forke).
With a great deal of what they said I am in entire accord. It is interesting, however, to note that one of the fathers of protection in this countiy, one of the admirers of Sir John A. Macdonald, who imposed protection on the country in 1S78, has had to speak with such utter frankness of what has grown up under the system. The system, he says, is not at fault; the system is a good one. But unfortunately there have been a large number of "growths" around the system. The question, to my mind, is whether a system can be characterized as good which brings about such unhappy results. However, I am not here to seek occasions for difference but to endeavour to find common ground of accord. It seems to me that we should pass this bill into committee of the whole House, or, if the government think it well, refer it to a special committee for further investigation and study. I indicate two courses of procedure, but I do not give my preference to either. But all the representatives of the people in this House should, I think, join in giving the principle of the bill their hearty support. Let no false impression go abroad from this House to any special interests in the country that there is any particular feeling of sympathy in any comer of the House, with those who, placed in strategic positions in the structure either of production or of distribution, propose to take advantage of such positions. Let that be clearly understood. We may differ as to methods; some may incline to one method of procedure and some to another. But let it be understood that the representatives of the Canadian people, no matter what place in this House they may occupy will not stand for extortion or exactions of more than a fair profit in business or in manufacture. Let us get the bill into committee, and, without any attempt to gain party advantage the one at the expense of the other, endeavour to develop the necessary machinery to make the legislation effective. The hon. member for South York anticipated some of the remarks I desired to make in this regard. The resources of civilization are not exhausted when we come to deal with combines and monopolies. Monopoly cannot raise an arrogant head in this country and lead the

Combines-Mr. McMaster
representatives of the people to understand that they, the monopolists, are masters of the situation and that nothing can be done. We control our ports and harbours, and if we find combinations of shippers who endeavour to charge all that the traffic will bear, and to stcfie and suffocate the commesce of tlie country, we can say to them: If you pursue such methods as these, not one ship of yours shall be allowed to tie up at any public* wharf. We can say to those who on the Great Lakes pursue such a policy that not a lock on the canal shall open until fair and just rates for the carriage of our natural and our industrial products shall be agreed upon. That is one weapon, and by no means a small one, which is in the hands of the government.

What about freight
rates?

I was just coming to freight rates; my hon. friend has anticipated me. The people of Canada own the greatest transportation system, in point of mileage, on this continent. Let it be known that those persons, whether middlemen or otherwise, who refuse to deal justly with their fellow men so far as distribution, the cost of distribution or the cost of manufacture are concerned, shall find it mighty difficult to move their goods on the railways of the people. And, last but not least, there is the tariff. As long as a tariff is maintained as an engine for raising revenue

and in my opinion a very expensive engine it is-let it be known that the tariff shall be used as a weapon to defend the rights of the people against the monopolists and that those who charge unjust and unfair prices for what they are able to produce under the shadow of the tariff wall may find that wall reduced or even cut down altogether, in order that it shall be impossible for them to charge their fellow Canadian citizens more than a fair price for a decent article.
These are some of the methods which I think might be incorporated in this bill. I invite to the support of this bill all those in this House who feel that the economic life of Canada is not what it should be. I do not propose that the government should abandon any rights to control freight rates, to control their ports or the tariff, which they now possess. If the government were omniscient the investigatory portions of this bill might be unnecessary, but as long as governments are composed of human beings they will not be either omnipotent or omniscient. Therefore, is there any more reasonable method to pursue than that indicated under
the bill-that there should be investigation, and after investigation, action? Whether the investigation should be carried on just as indicated in the bill; whether the action should not be rather larger, rather broader than as narrow as indicated in the bill, are matters which we can discuss, I respectfully suggest, Mr. Speaker, better in committee than when we are sitting as the House. But I do think that this bill deserves the support of all the representatives of the people. I would be glad to see notice given to all monopolists and combinesters in this country, by the unanimous vote of this House, that the heart and the mind of the representatives of the Canadian people are behind this legislation in order that it may have a fair chance and a fair field to bring about the desired end, namely, not the reduction of prices irrespective of what the goods cost, but a fair deal for the consumer as well as for the producer.	,

Mr. Speaker, there will be ample opportunity to discuss the details of this bill when we go into committee, this the second reading is the occasion for discussion of the general principles of the bill. For that reason I am going to say only a few words this afternoon. But, coming from a city that has had a great deal to do with the Board of Commerce-perhaps more to do with it than all the rest of the municipalities of Canada put together because we have had more applications before it-I would like to make a few remarks regarding the proposed legislation.
I would like to help the government in the work they have before them, but I am sorry that they have seen fit to bring down such a bill as that now before us. If you read the bill from cover to cover; if you carefully examine the definition of "combines," "registrar," and so on; if you look into the machinery provided for the enforcement of the act, it will be seen that the general principle of the bill is based on the old Board of Commerce and the Combines and Fair Prices Act. The denouncing of capital is very popular with some, particularly at election time. Personally I would not want to be an employer to-day, having regard to the high taxes and the high prices which are general throughout the country. The lot of the employer or of the capitalist is not an easy one, by any means. I know a great many capitalists interested in private enterprises who work as hard as, if not harder than, any labouringjnan in Canada, who spend large sums to improve their business, and who in many cases give a lot of their money away to the public. In some respects they are more
Combines-Mr. Church

sinned against, than sinning. I say it is a popular act with some hon. members of this House to denounce from the housetops, trusts and combines and restraints of trade. We had a speech this afternoon from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock).
