No gentleman in the late election went further than he did concerning what would be done to the combines and trusts if he was returned as the member for South Toronto. This subject is a predominant one in Toronto, particularly among the working classes. I may say that the working classes in Canada have themselves done more to regulate the trusts and combines by not buying when prices are increased than all the legislation I have seen. We hear a great deal about the big interests, particularly at election time; it has been said that we on this side are the allies of the big interests, that was said, indeed, by the hon. Minister of Labour himself in the election campaign in South Toronto.
Now, what are these "big interests" that are referred to? They are, first, the transportation and shipping interests; second, the manufacturers and the Manufacturers' Association; third, the banking interests and trusts and combines along these lines. What has the minister done to regulate these trusts during the two years that he has been in office? There is no country in the world to-day in which the big interests flourish like a green bay tree, without let or hindrance, as they do in the Dominion of Canada. Canada is the happy hunting ground for all these American trusts and combines. Take the restaurant trust to-day-Child's, Bowles' and all these places. They are well established in the big cities of the United States, and they have crossed to Canada. They are subject to public regulation in the United States; inquiries have been made respecting them and prosecutions taken against them to bring down the prices, but nothing of that land has been done in Canada.
It has been said that the party system in Canada has fallen down in its regulation of trusts. I am soriy that this question has been made the political football of this party or that party. In fact, both political parties are in the same boat in this respect; they have done what they could to try to regulate these trusts and combines on behalf of the public but have failed. I wish to give the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a certain amount of credit, in connection with this particular matter, for bringing down this bill for debate for he has long been a student of labour. Hon. members criticize the party system for not having done something to 
regulate the trusts and combines; I wish to criticize the United Farmers of Ontario and the group system for having fallen down in this matter. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has said that there is a shipping trust on the Great Lakes. So there is. And there is a sugar trust. Anyone who will take Houston's Financial Annual will see the large number of mergers that have been formed in recent years. The city of Toronto spent about $10,000 at the request of this Board of Commerce, of which the present Minister of Labour was one of the members, to secure data for them. There was a general complaint among the working classes and those receiving small salaries that they could not get a good lunch in a restaurant under anywhere from 60 or 75 cents to $1. A bit of a sandw'ich would cost 25 or 30 cents; com, which could be bought at about 15 to 18 cents a dozen, would be sold at 35 or 40 cents each; tomatoes retailing at 35 cents a basket would sell at 35 cents a plate in some restaurants and hotds. The women's organizations sent a deputation to the Toronto City Council and Board of Control; they filled the council chamber-several hundred of them-and asked that we should do something regarding the prices of certain food products. It was pointed out to them what the law was, that section 498 of the Criminal Code had been suspended because of the Board of Commerce Act of 1919 and the Combines and Fair Prices Act. So the medical health officer, Dr. Hastings, was requested to make a survey of the situation in Toronto, at the request of the Board of Commerce which he did at great expense to the taxpayer. He made a survey and collected enough evidence to fill a trunk. It was sent down to the Board of Commerce at Ottawa, who filed and pigeon holed this elaborate report, but nothing further was done. They simply passed the buck to somebody else, as the military authorities say-all that could be done under that particular act.
I give the men who proposed that act credit for being sincere, but with all due respect that act failed, and for many reasons. The Board of Commerce legislation was founded very largely on the successful carrying on of the United States Federal Trade Commission, but the Board of Commerce never got going, and I believe the same will be true of this new board that is to be appointed-I do not believe it will ever get going. Before it gets going the skilled lawyers of the trusts will raise some technicalities and have the legislation before the Privy Council. Some clever lawyer will find

Combines-Mr. Church
a, flaw in the drafting, notwithstanding that it has been drafted by the Justice department, and we shall find it declared to be ultra vires of this parliament. The Board of Commerce was founded largely on popular clamour to regulate prices after the war. Popular clamour demanded action by parliament in 1918 and 1919, and in 1919 two acts were passed, but the main features of the Board of Commerce legislation, and the main functions of the board of 1919 never came into operation, owing to members of the board resigning, and owing to the fact that no action was taken on their reports. So the real working functions of the board of 1919 were never performed, and I predict that this new board will never perform its functions either, but will simply become a cypher. In other words the Board of Commerce Act was, and this act will be, "still-born" so far as practical results go.
I may say that profit control was one
of the very last functions the Board of Commerce considered-but profit control, should be the main function in the regulation of prices and trusts and combines. The Board of Commerce no doubt did some good work. Mr. O'Connor did very good work in connection with profiteering, and the bacon extortion, and I venture to say that if some war profiteers had been prosecuted, better results would have been obtained. But the war profiteers were in a preferred class in this country. They got away not only with profits but with titles as well.
If I may be permitted a suggestion to the government I would advise them to repeal altogether the legislation of 1919 and adopt some practical legislation such as they have in the United States-the grand jury scheme of inquiry-under which some four hundred and eighty combines, trusts and mergers were prosecuted in one year by federal and state authorities. Take Judge Landis of the city of Chicago; he prosecuted the Standard Oil combine and imposed a fine on that corporation of 850,000,000 under federal legislation. That was practical legislation, not legislation under which you ran round in a circle and when you had got round it handed it over to the provincial Attorney General or passed the buck to another.
The provincial Attorney General in Ontario is in politics and does nothing but talk.
This matter was put up to him but he said: No, let the Dominion government look after it. We laid a bill of indictment before Mr. Justice Kelly and a jury, and we were told that the Crown prosecutor would not take the case, first, because the Attorney General would not approve, secondly, because
he had no power inasmuch as the Criminal Code had been superseded by the Board of Commerce Act, and thirdly, because the applicant, the city of Toronto, would have to put up a bond as security for costs and bringing the witnesses there. But in the United States they did get results by the grand jury system of inquiry into trusts and combines and got results quickly.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that some of these mergers are good things. I could name several of them that have been good for the country ; when they cut down the overhead and reduce the price of the article. Many of them have done good, but the majority of them have done wrong, and several of them are all wrong and should be regulated. The producer has the law on his side. It is always there in many ways to protect him. The law always favours the producer. But the five-and-ten-dollar consumer, the poor man, finds the legislation all against him. Take the Lords Day Act, for instance, if a man is rich he can buy ice cream and a box of cigars for Sunday, but the poor man cannot have these luxuries on Sunday because he can only buy a cone or one cigar at a time. It is the same with trusts and combines. A poor man cannot get anywhere in his attack on them. If he wants to lay a charge he is told by the Crown: You will please put up security for costs, and so forth. I would suggest that the government adopt the grand jury system of inquiry as set out in the report of Judge Landis of Chicago. He did a great deal of good work, advised the federal authorities and got results a thousandfold.
I should like to propose this amendment if the government would be good enough to consider it. Of course, I know it cannot be moved to-day, but I should like to bring it to the attention of the government. It has been asked for by many grand juries. I know that a couple of grand juries made a recommendation something like the amendment I have drafted. I propose that the following be added to the bill as section 37, and I shall move this amendment in Committee of the Whole House:
(37) Any grand jury at any sittings of the General Sessions of the Peace, or any grand jury at any sitting of the High Court of Justice, or any grand jury duly and lawfully convened in any province of Canada, may exercise as respects any person or any property within such province any power which by this act may be exercised by the registrar or any commission appointed under this act, without obligation, however, to report to any minister of the Crown, and with power to make a presentment in accordance with the facts found by it.
What I would suggest is that the government repeal the Board of Commerce Act of 1919 and the Combines and Fair Prices Act
Combines-Mr. Church

of 1919, and go back to the old law, section 498 of the Criminal Code. Let us broaden out that section by such an amendment as I have suggested, giving the grand juries power to go into these questions. After all is said and done, the government of the day can do very little in a matter of this kind. There are many problems which governments cannot handle in days of stress and strain like these. There are many problems that the government cannot solve legally or otherwise except with the aid of Providence-and while the government may try to do the best they can and are sometimes criticized unfairly, and sometimes insincerely, the best action to take in this matter is to decentralize the problem. There is nothing like the old law of supply and demand. The people of New York state have been teaching a lesson to the sugar combine and women organizations have been established in New York state to fight that combine by not buying sugar in order to force the price down. The same thing happened over here many years ago among the working classes as they refused to buy certain necessities of life because of the high prices. So while the government may endeavour to do its part, it cannot do all, and it is better for it to decentralize and leave this matter to those who have the necessary time, ability and knowledge-the judges, Crown officers, grand juries and municipal officers. Give them a chance of looking into these questions; and also give the grand juries the opportunity I have suggested, because there is nothing like a little publicity in these matters, and the grand juiy will get results that this bill will never get.
I spoke of the city of Toronto's experience with the Board of Commerce and pointed out that we got no action at all. Bearing that in mind it was a funny thing to me to hear the speech of the Minister of Labour this afternoon. He was a member of that Board of Commerce. I do not wish to be unfair to him, but I understand that after all the members of the board had resigned he still remained a member for four months and drew his salary. If he did not believe the board was fulfilling its functions, he should have resigned and not drawn the salary which he did.
Apparently the hon. gentleman is not aware that I was not the last member of the Board of Commerce to go. Mr. O'Connor left the Board of Commerce after I did.

I gladly accept the hon. minister's statement, but he was a judge on

the board and acted although he now says his powers were curtailed. I do not know about this particular problem but I do know that when a trunk load of evidence was sent to the Board of Commerce in regard to the operations of certain combines, including American restaurants in the city of Toronto, it was without result. The health officer of that city at the request of the Board of Commerce spent thousands of dollars in collecting evidence with respect to combines of many kinds -restaurant services, boots and shoes, clothing and others. When that evidence was sent down to the Board of Commerce why did they not act? Instead of acting they moved in a circle and wound up by asking the attorney general of the province to institute proceedings. Well, the people of Toronto got disgusted, and what did they do? They laid a complaint before the Board of Police Commissioners stating that exorbitant prices in restaurants were being charged, and excessive prices for milk and the other commodities I have named, which are really necessities of life. That board took prompt action. In the city of Toronto restaurants, for example, cannot operate except under license from the police commissioners. So Colonel Denison and his colleagues, including Judge Winchester and myself, summoned the managers of these American restaurants before the police board and threatened to cancel their licenses unless the rates they were charging were cut in two within one week. Action in the desired direction promptly followed. Before the expiration of the allotted time the prices charged for coffee, toast, vegetables, eggs, and other articles had been reduced by 33 1-3 per cent. This shows that you can get action if you only go the right way about it. I really believe that if we could have periodic inquiries by the grand jury as in the United States into excessive prices we would really make more headway. Personally, I do not think it is fair for the government to introduce a bill of this character so late in the session. The principle involved here is exactly the same as in the legislation of 1919, but the difficulty seems to be for the lawyers to draft a statute in such a way that it will not be declared ultra vires of this parliament.
The tariff is blamed for the condition of affairs that is complained of. In my opinion the tariff is not responsible. The Mother Country is a free trade country and yet mergers, trusts and combines flourish over there. The United States has a protective tariff but over there they enforce the law against trusts and combines. As I have already said the United States federal attorney general, with the assist-

Combines-Mr. Church
anoe of the state attorney general, has prosecuted some 485 combines in one year over there resulting in the imposition upon them of penalties amounting to millions of dollars in the aggregate and the control of prices and mergers. Therefore, you cannot blame the tariff for the existence of these combines. The tariff is blamed for almost everything but in my opinion it is not responsible for this particular problem. The difference between the proposed legislation and that enacted in 1919 is that in the present bill you can by order in council amend the tariff. If a combine is taking advantage of it, or you can revoke a patent found to be operating injuriously to the public you can do that already now in another way. It is also provided that if the Attorney General of a province does not enforce the report of a registrar, the Solicitor General may act in certain cases.
The act of 1919 and the present bill will fail in effect for the same reason that the Board of Commerce failed. Undoubtedly there is a demand for action of some kind. A great many trusts and combines are flourishing in this country. The shipping qombine, for example, seems to be most active both in the matter of freight and passenger rates. Formerly one could travel from Toronto to Niagara Falls for 81.25 return but that rate has been increased to $3 and over. Freight lates on fruit, vegetables and farm products carried to cities and towns on the shores of lake Erie and lake Ontario have also been enhanced. The small freight and passenger boats which in former days used to operate with great advantage and convenience to the public have been frozen out by this combine. The matter should be looked into by Mr. Raney the Attorney General of Ontario. This combine, which is a restraint on shipping, could be investigated and remedial action taken if the provincial Attorney General were so inclined under section 498 of the Criminal Code. The same is true of many other combines that are flourishing like a green bay tree.
There is a question involved here as to the power of parliament to enact such legislation in view of the decision given by the Privy Council in 1921 in the case of the Attorney General of Canada vs. the Attorney General of Alberta. It would appear from that judgment that it is very doubtful whether this parliament can enforce such legislation as this proposed bill inasmuch as property and civil rights within a province is exclusively a matter for the provincial legislature, and that the federal authority cannot erect a board competent to make regulations affecting trade and commerce which will be
of merely local application. This parliament can, however, regulate trade and commerce if its regulations are of general application and for the general advantage of Canada. If parliament goes to the extent proposed in this new legislation before us to-day into the matter of property and civil rights it is very doubtful if it can enforce the act by merely declaring that to violate it is a crime. I would suggest that the proper course to take would be to broaden out section 498 of the Criminal Code so as to enable a grand jury to investigate these and declare the maintenance of mergers, trusts and combines of a wrongful nature a crime. One of the ablest county court judges we had in Toronto was the late Judge Winchester, who was also a police commissioner. Some fifteen or sixteen years ago, he, together with Colonel Denison, police magistrate, took action under this section 498 against certain trusts. They sent down and seized the books of a particular trust complained of and within twenty-four hours those identified with that trust amended their regulations and reduced their prices. As it is now, section 498 of the Criminal Code is practically inoperative. Some time ago a prosecution was started against the milk combine in Toronto under section 498. A bill was preferred against a milk combine, but Mr. Justice Kelly and the crown prosecutor, Mr. White, refused to consider a bill of indictment, because, they said, the powers given under the Criminal Code, section 498, had been superseded by those conferred on the Board of Commerce. I would suggest to the government that they carefully confer with the Justice department and see whether, by broadening section 498 and bringing into operation the functions of grand juries, properly convened, action cannot be taken in the desired direction rather than pass legislation of this character. In that way no harm would be done to capital, to labour, or to any public interest and combines, trusts and restraints of trade would be subject to some practical, useful and effective public control.

Before the second reading of this bill passes I would like to dispel an impression which may have been created in the minds of hon. gentlemen by certain references of an hon. member to the Canadian Press. The remarks in question were offered by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), and were very ably replied to by the Prime Minister whose statement I am glad to substantiate. Unfortunately those remarks have been accepted and commented on by subsequent speakers in this debate. In the first
25S8
Combines-Mr. Rinjret

place, I would like to correct the idea that the Canadian Press can prevent the publication of a newspaper in any city in this country, also that this organization is in any sense a "combine of opinion". It is not by any means in the power of the Canadian Press to prevent the publication of any paper in Canada. The only thing they can do, and which they have done in< certain cases, is to deny to certain papers applying for it the privilege of the interchange of news which is enjoyed by those papers composing the Canadian Press. That matter I will deal with at some length later on. But the Canadian Press, contrary to the view expressed by some hon. members opposite, is in no sense a "combine of opinion" because the opinion expressed by any paper has no place whatever in the exchange of news among the different papers concerned. What the Canadian Press does is to furnish to its members news of the events transpiring in different localities in Canada. This is merely carrying out on a larger scale the arrangement which formerly existed between the newspapers of Montreal and the newspapers of Quebec for the exchange of local news. In accordance with this arrangement a newspaper in Quebec would wire to its Montreal confrere local happenings of interest, and the Montreal newspaper would reciprocate by sending to Quebec news of interest from its own neighbourhood. It was thought that the papers in different cities of Canada might agree to an exchange of news and that great advantage might accrue, not only to the papers but also to the reading public, because it would enable the different papers to carry the news at a cheaper rate. But again I say, never has the opinion of a paper been called in question. Take for instance the report of the Canadian House of Commons. These reports are published by Tory papers and by Liberal papers and by Progressive organs, because they are merely a compendium of what takes place in the House. If a paper wishes to comment on speeches made in the House, or measures that are being presented by the government, it is for them to engage a special Ottawa correspondent or to take it up in the editorial columns. There is no question of opinion in the alleged combine of the Canadian press. A Tory paper that is a party to that association may later be bought by the Liberal party or by an independent party, yet it would retain the privileges it enjoys in the Canadian Press. I repeat it is not in the power of the Canadian Press to prevent any paper from starting publication in a city where papers 
belonging to the Canadian Press Association already exist. The only situation that is created is that a paper starting in without the services of the Canadian Press would naturally be placed under a certain handicap, and possibly in that regard the Canadian Press may come more or less within the scope of the bill now before the House. There is not the slightest understanding between any of the papers concerned in the Canadian Press with regard to the rates of advertisement, or the price the paper will charge for copies. I would submit that this news service cannot be handled by a private company. It might be said that it would be better if a private company would undertake to organize a service of that kind and to place it on the market at a certain price so that every paper in the country could buy it. But a private company, not having the machinery and not having the benefit of the organization of the newspapers in different parts of the country could not hope to undertake a service of that kind at a price moderate enough to allow any of the papers to use it. It will also be understood that a service of that kind cannot be unlimited in number of members forming the association. The principle of it is an interchange of news. If you have in that association a paper whose service is limited, and it enjoys the news service of a larger paper for which it does not give a corresponding news service, there certainly would be a lack in the organization that would not be for the good of the newspapers concerned generally or for the good of the public that it is intended to serve.
On the other hand, we cannot forget that this association gets a subsidy from the government, and it looks very much as if it came to a point where the government was subsidizing a certain number of papers ard leaving it in the hands of those papers to refuse admission of other papers in their association. I may say, quoting from memory, that article 7 of the charter of the Canadian Press of 1914 grants to the association the privilege of establishing regulations for the admission and expulsion of members. Possibly there is there too great a liberty given to the association. I would think that if the charter were amended in such a way that the Canadian Press could not refuse admission of papers applying for admission under certain conditions, we might remedy that part of it. But as I am connected with a paper which is now in the association of the Canadian Press, I thought it would be well, before the bill is read the second time, to give this explana-

Combines-Mr. Baxter
tion to the House. Personally I do not think,
outside of that point, that these papers are enjoying a subsidy of public money, I do not think there is anything wrong with the arrangement at all. I would say that if this bill is given effect to it might form the subject of an investigation, but I am quite sure the Canadian Press could withstand an investigation, and could show that its alleged combine is merely an arrangement whereby the Canadian public are getting news from alt over the Dominion, not of a political or contentious character, but merely facts, and they are getting it at a cheaper price than they could if that association did not exist.
I fully agree with the principle of this bill. Some hon. member asked last night, what is the principle of the bill? I think the principle is clear. It is giving the taxpayer an efficient weapon against combines. It has been argued against the bill that it is useless because section 498 of the Criminal Code deals with combines. It has also been argued against the bill that the proceedings provided are too long and of a circuitous character. It has also been argued that the registrar should have wider powers and also a penalizing power. Other arguments have been presented to the effect that this bill could be abused, and that we must protect trade against any demand for inquiry that would not be warranted, and also that we must have secrecy in the proceedings in order to prevent blackmailing or anything of that character. I think all these arguments presented against the bill answer themselves. The reason why the proceedings are of the character the bill provides for, and the reason why the registrar is not given too extended power, is precisely to prevent what other members are afraid the bill might do; that is that it might serve, in the hands of an unscrupulous man or group of unscrupulous men, a wrong purpose. I think it is perfectly right that the registrar should not have absolute power, and that his power should be merely, as the bill provides, to establish an inquiry. It is also perfectly right that whatever company is inquired into should have the right to present its defence. I believe that the argument presented by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that it was a wrong principle to give a chance to the accused party to know of an accusation and give that party time to answer the accusation, is a very wrong argument and altogether un-British. I think the bill is along the right lines. This bill gives the public an opportunity to apply to a registrar for an inquiry, something which it could not do under the criminal code on account of the expenses that
would be involved. It gives to the registrar power to restrict that inquiry, but it gives to the accused parties an opportunity to present their defence. I have sympathy for the proposal that has been made by some hon. members, including the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler), that a certain secrecy should be kept over these proceedings as long as the accused party has not been found guilty, because this would be the be= means to prevent any group of men from using this bill, not to fine a combine but merely to serve some other purpose.
In conclusion, I hope this bill will attain its end, not only by providing means to suppress existing combines, but, if it proves an efficient weapon in the hands of the peopD, by preventing the formation of combines in future. I believe that this should be the aim of all legislation, not only to remedy what evil already exists, but to prevent that evil from spreading in the future.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
After the number of speeches that we have heard upon this subject, which is an important one, I do not know whether I am acting wisely in continuing _to occupy the time of the House, as very much of the discussion will properly proceed upon the details of the measure when we are considering it in committee section by section. Yet there are some general observations which have occurred to me and which I feel are fundamental with respect to the measure, and that is my excuse for troubling the House after the debate has already proceeded so extensively.
In the first place, even at the risk of uttering some generalities, I think I may say that the speakers have been generally, if not entirely, in accord in recognizing as perhaps fundamental that combines, trusts and mergers are not necessarily injurious to the public interest. On the other hand, it is common experience that under certain circumstances, and carried on in a certain way, combines, trusts and mergers may produce a very great-injury to the public. I think we can all see that, in the very formation of great aggregations of capital or industry, the world is slowly working out the problem of co-operation which, in some form or other, perhaps one or perhaps many generations after the present time, will find a different method of adjusting
Combines-Mr. Baxter

human relationships from that which we now possess. It is not unnatural perhaps from this side of the House for me to take the traditionally Conservative view of desiring to be assured of what the next step is going to be before I take it. It is not to be wondered at that a certain portion of the community, which I might describe as radical, desires to take some extraordinary step regardless of consequences and rather for the sake of experimentation. Between the two seems to lie the traditionally Liberal view-I do not know whether I interpret it aright-of not saying whether they are going to take any step or not, but of waiting for things to turn up.
I do not wish to be understood as being opposed to legislation of the character which has been introduced in the House. Some remarks have fallen from the lips of hon. members rather intimating that there was no sincerity^ on the part of the previous government in dealing with this question. Some have said that the previous methods have not been effective. Really, Mr. Speaker, I would rather attribute that feature of the discussion, which we have heard in this Chamber, more to a desire to exploit the subject for political capital than to any real wish to bring something to bear upon the present measure and to discuss it on its merits, offering, if they can be made, helpful suggestions for the working out of the act. The past must always be the past, and I trust we are living in the present and looking toward the future; and it is for us, if we do not think that a suggested remedial measure reaches what is really perhaps a danger point in our civilization, to contribute something to the perfecting of that measure. I intend that what I say to-night shall be directed to that end, because before I conclude I trust I shall be able to make some suggestions which I believe would enable the present government and this parliament more effectively to deal with a question of this character than we are able to do under present circumstances.
Among the criticisms that we have heard of the past legislation was the remark of one hon. member that we had now got legislation with a kick in it, as he expressed it. I think I may fairly claim for past administrations, whether they have been Liberal or Conservative, that they have each and all recognized the difficulties which may be presented by some form of commercial combination and have each put forward some means of remedying this state of affairs, which means was thought to be adequate at the time it was promoted. I think the House could fairly agree to that; and it will be conceded, I have no doubt, that the measure introduced in the

time of Sir John A. Macdonald was quite sufficient to meet the evils that appeared in his time; that later legislation which was introduced by my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was believed by him and his party to be adequate for such evils as existed at that time; and that when we come down to the Board of Commerce and the combines legislation my right hon. friend who leads this side of the House (Mr. Meighen) was presenting what was believed to be the most adequate and the latest development in legislation for dealing with difficulties of the character that was being experienced in that day. Surely we must give some credit for a little honour and sincerity of purpose in public life; and I think that the House would do much better to trace the legislation step by step to see where improvements have been made and to find out what gaps, if any, have been left unfilled, and view the present proposition in the light of that history and present experience, with the object of getting some measure, if the present one is not the best, that will be adequate to meet the situation. It is entirely in that spirit, as I say, that I wish to approach the question.
Now, we have to start practically from the Board of Commerce Act and the Combines and Fair Prices Act. There was legislation that I do not think can fairly be described as a wooden gun; it did not in any way lack a kick. The power was there for investigation, for prosecution, for punishment. If the old code provisions, about which I hope to say something before I get through, were not sufficient, at all events the government in 1919 took steps, by two reciprocal measures, to rid the country so far as possible of all unfair dealing in the necessaries of life and in articles of trade and commerce. I do not understand, I cannot find from the records, that a single criticism was offered at that time as to the possible ineffectiveness of the legislation. There was some criticism that the legislation was going too far, but we never heard, I think, on the floor of this House the suggestion that the legislation was in any way outside the competence of this parliament. Now, what happened? The legislation was called into question. We must expect that; every interest that is struck by legislation will naturally turn to the courts and look for relief. Certain interested parties did that; the case was ultimately submitted to the Privy Council, and whether we like it or not, whether or not we think it ought to be the law, we are bound to accept their decision as the law in this respect, and there is

Combines-Mr. Baxter
no appeal for us except to the supreme lawmaking assembly, the parliament of Great Britain.
What did the Privy fcouncil decide? I will not trouble the House by reading lengthy extracts from the judgment, but I think I can put it on this ground: The Privy Council recognized, as it must recognize, the division of powers as between the Dominion and the provinces as laid down by the British North America Act; that in the enumeration of powers vested solely in the province we have property and civil rights within the provinces, and that there is no power in this parliament to trench upon property and civil rights except in some mode ancillary to carrying out some one or more of the powers which are expressly and exclusively confided to this parliament by the British North America Act. I think that any layman, and a great many lawyers, in looking at the British North America Act and studying the allocation of subjects which are within the exclusive jurisdiction of parliament, would have said that the words "trade and commerce" were ample to confer all possible and requisite jurisdiction upon this parliament. But a decision of the Privy Council has laid it down that the vast business of insurance, which has grown so mightily in the last few decades, is not a subject falling within trade and commerce. The Privy Council went much further when the Combines and Fair Prices Act was submitted to it. The Privy Council said that unless the subjects dealt with fell within trade and commerce, this parliament had no power over them at all. It went even a step farther and declared that you could not decide that a thing that fell within the class of "property and civil rights" within a province was noxious and, having decided that, take it out of the class of property and civil rights by calling it an infraction of the criminal law. Whether we like this as a decision or whether we do not, it is the law that binds us today and it' is the principle by which the act submitted by the right hon. Prime Minister must be judged. So that one of the objects of my address this evening is to clear away, if I can, what I humbly think are some misconceptions that prevail in this Chamber with regard to the power and the ability of the measure which has been presented.
I have heard hon. members discussing a subject into the details of which I do not propose to enter, namely, the regulation by an association of newspapers of a certain franchise. I know that some hon. members honestly feel that all that it is necessary to do is to get this bill enacted into law and that they
will then be able to use the investigator and resort to the courts in order to obtain a franchise for a newspaper which is now being denied a franchise. Well, all I can say is that in the light of the decisions to which I have referred, that is a complete misconception of the law. I am not afraid of being treated as a prophet; in fact, there is no prophecy involved in it. You can adopt every syllable of this bill and there will be no relief for that newspaper situation. Let us pass to something else entirely different. This law professes to strike at, possibly, combinations in insurance, but it will be futile in any attempt to deal with that question because insurance has been declared not to be a part of trade and commerce by the highest legal authority in the Empire, and merely putting insurance in this bill will not make it a part of trade and commerce. Unless you legislate with respect to trade and commerce in its widest and amplest sense, you are not legislating at all; there is no power here to deal with the matter. Where then, is the power? The Privy Council has said that it resides in the local legislatures. Unfortunately for the objects of this bill, it does; and before I get through I shall possibly suggest a remedy with regard to that.
Let us now come to something that gets much nearer home so far as a good many members of this House and a go. d many of their constituents are concerned. Mention was made in the course of the debate of the question of milk supply. I have not the slightest doubt that hon. members within the sound of my voice think that if this bill goes through it will be possible to stop any unfair or oppressive combination with regard to the distribution of milk or the fixing of prices for milk. But you cannot do it. If this parliament had the power, the bill would be effective, but the bill fails because parliament constitutionally has not the power. The sale of milk, the sale of butter, of eggs, of ordinary dairy products, of most of the things that we eat or drink or wear, form incidents in the law of property and civil rights which has by the wisdom of our forefathers been allocated to the provinces. Hon. members will recall last year the difficulty that was experienced with regard to a wheat board. That was another attempt of Union government to do a thing that was strongly desired by a part of this country; it failed in precisely the same way. Hon. members know the difficulties that have been experienced since in trying to get corresponding legislation from the provinces in order that a wheat board might be galvanized into partial life. The very same thing that creates that difficulty

Combines-Mr. Baxter

creates this one: you are simply up against the powers of the provincial legislatures and the want of power of this parliament.
Banks and banking. You have there a subject that belongs to the Dominion. You may pass legislation of this character dealing with banks and banking because you have control of the subject and you can pass any law that you want to with regard to the subject. With respect to insurance, as I have said, you cannot. Retail business within a province this parliament cannot touch because it does not fall under any of the heads of the powers that belong to this parliament. Wholesale business if limited to a single province would be equally out of the scope of the legislation, and I have already made a remark about the newspaper situation.
Now what is the remedy for this? In my judgment, and I am giving it for what it is worth, the proper way to reach this subject is to get the power in this parliament to deal with what is a very important phase of national life. I do not regard the compact of confederation as a thing that came into force on the 1st day of July, 1867, and that has never to be altered. I realize the immense difficulties there would be in getting the consent of the provinces to approach the Imperial parliament and have a resettling of those distributions of power, but I think we have got to come to it some day. I am not going to discuss by itself in any way the question of the wheat board that we had last winter, but I say that if wheat control is a necessary thing for Canada, if that be demonstrated then the obvious, the logical, the necessary thing to do is to go where the power can be given and get the power given to this parliament to deal with a question of that kind by Canada, instead of having it split up among the several provinces and become utterly ineffective. Just in the same way, if I am right in my interpretation of the judgment of the Privy Council, and I think I am, the remedy that ought to be applied today is not the enacting of legislation which is going to fall far, far short of the expectations of this House, is going to fall far, far short of the provisions that are contained in it, so far as effectiveness is concerned; the remedy is to get the provinces to co-operate and to ask the Imperial parliament to change the distribution of powers between the federal and the local legislatures and give the power to this body so that efficient legislation may be enacted. We are going to have, and have in increasing measure as time goes on, trusts and combines, mergers and monopolies, and it seems to me almost farcical to suggest that

they ever can or will be adequately dealt with by provincial legislation. Then if the power is not here, and the Privy Council has said that it is not here except in rare instances, again I repeat the obvious thing is to take the proper steps to get the power so that this parliament may function in accord with the will of the people.
But entirely apart from that I would like to take perhaps a few minutes to discuss what might be done at the present time, without seeking any delay, that would afford some relief, would give some power and would in my opinion be more effective than the measure that is proposed; in other words would d) very much the same thing but in a different sort of way. Reference has been made to section 498 of the Criminal Code. Reference has also been made to a judgment recently in an Ontario court, and to the observations of the Deputy Minister of Justice upon that decision. In my judgment-it may not be worth much but it is the best I have got- the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice is absolutely right and the obiter of the Chief Justice of Ontario-perhaps it was more than that-that the code provision was ultra vires is, I humbly submit, not a correct view of the law. I prefer and believe to be correct the judgment of the majority of the court and the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice. But this code provision which has been ii force now for a great many years has never been a wooden gun. It has never been an ineffective weapon. It has been simply, readily applied, easily operated, and it may surprise hon. members of the House to realize that it has been invoked at least with fair frequency and on the whole with a very great deal of success. If my hon. friends will take the trouble to take any modem book on Canadian criminal jurisprudence, turn to section 498 and look at the list of cases that are cited as having been decided under it, they will find that in the great majority of these cases the prosecutions were successful. I have not pretended-I did not think it worth while

to make an exhaustive digest of the cases because I realize that while parliament is a court in one sense, yet about the last thing that parliament desires is to hear a lawyer talking shop, and therefore I do not want to make a long bead-roll of cases. But I might point out that there was a wheat case in Manitoba. It is known as the Gage case. There the prosecution failed. But why did it fail? Because the court held, or the single judge before whom it was tried held, and the appellate court felt they could not interfere with him, that an agreement to exact a profit of one cent

cause he had formulated a different one. I would be driven to this position: I would have to say that it must be a matter of considerable doubt, and that the question could not be resolved until the opinion of the highest appellate tribunal in the Empire had been taken on the subject. Because, after all, there is no very great difference in the reasoning power among the members of my profession. It is just as possible for one man to read the judgment of the Privy Council and draw his deductions as it is for another; and I would not lightly let go of my opinion which I may say I have not formed except after a very great deal of study of the question. I believe that I am absolutely right, though I would be sorry to assert that in such a broad way if I were confronted with an opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice just as stoutly asserting the opposite.
Now, in the course of the Board of Commerce case the Privy Council pointed out pretty well what this parliament might do. In summing up the legislation of the Combines and Fair Prices Act they pointed out that it authorized the board, under that act, to restrict in cases of food, clothing and fuel, accumulations of these necessaries of life beyond the amount reasonably required in the case of a private person for his household not less than in the case of a trader for his business. They pointed out further that this was an interference in normal times with property and civil rights; that the authority of parliament to legislate for the regulation of trade and commerce does not, by itself, enable interference with particular trades in which Canadians would, apart from any right of interference conferred by these words, be free to engage in the provinces. They further said that legislation implies a claim of title in the cases of non-traders as well as of traders to make orders prohibiting the accumulation of certain articles required for everyday life, and the withholding of such articles from sale at prices to be defined by the board, whenever they exceed the amount of material which appears to the board to be required for domestic purposes or ordinary purposes of business. The board was authorized, they say, to deal with individual cases, and not merely as the result of applying principles to be laid down as of general application.
Now, what is the present legislation? It is simply authorizing not a board but a registrar to deal with individual cases and is not merely the result of applying the principles to be laid down as of general application. The Prime Minister has, I think, considerably improved the structure of his bill by striking

words out of the combination section leaving so much to the opinion of the registrar. But still the expression "combine," as defined by the bill, is to be what? It is:
-to have reference to such combines immediately hereinafter defined as have operated or are likely to operate to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or otherwise.
Limited as aforesaid the expression that is used in the bill is to be deemed to include certain things which are enumerated. I want to point out that while I, in common with every other member of this House, would be glad to see effective legislation which would prevent combinesters from attaining an object which they intended to reach in the future, yet when I read this language "have operated or are likely to operate," I realize that it is beyond the power of parliament to make a criminal act out of something that has not been committed. If this bill goes through in this form to the Privy Council, the moment they see that language they will say, "You cannot invoke the criminal law' to punish a man for what he has not yet done. You cannot with one foot step into the domain of provincial right, and place the other foot upon the bed rock of the Criminal Code, and try to straddle the question in that way. You tried it once with the Combines and Fair Prices Act, and we upset that; you cannot come back and try it under this slightly changed form of words, for the change is very slight."
What I am appealing to the House to consider is not at all the interests of any one who seeks to oppress the people, or the interests of any one who seeks to interfere with the trade and commerce or business of the country, and not the interests of any one who strives to make a purely partisan question out of this measure. I believe that the measure will go through, but I am trying to drive home to hon. members the fact-and they might as well know it before they vote for the bill-that when they have set the seal of legislation upon this measure they will have accomplished practically nothing, so far as effectiveness is concerned. They will have done one thing. They will have voted an indirect subsidy that will not be paid wholly out of the exchequer of this country, but that will be paid by scores of contributors throughout Canada to gentleman of my cloth, who will have an opportunity of discussing the defects of this measure before court after court, until it reaches the Privy Council, and in the meantime, once you get a case launched towards the Privy Council, you will have absolutely no attempt to enforce the law until

Combines-Mr. Baxter
that case is decided. You will have a veritable fit of paralysis.
My hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) was not able in his speech to accurately define the measure. He got a little bit off the track and was trying to put the blame on my right hon. leader. He has not described to us yet any nefarious device that my right hon. friend invented or made use of to prevent the Board of Commerce Act, or the Combines and Fair Prices Act, from working, but he says it did not work. The reason it did not work was that when the question was raised, and when the question was on its way to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, it would have been blind folly to have started prosecutions all over the country which might, and, as the result shows, would have been upset in their conclusions by that decision. I would ask if there is anything more specific in What the minister charged than what he has already said. I think the reason I have given is a complete answer to the remarks that he made, as I thought rather unfairly, trying to throw upon an individual blame for something which, if there is blame at all in connection with it, is due to the Fathers of Confederation, who, perhaps somewhat unwisely, divided the legislative power between the Dominion and the provinces. My right hon. friend can scarcely be accused of that, and I do not know that any one political party can be accused of it. We are learning and we are developing, and I am suggesting that there is a way out of the difficulty by a reallocation of those powers. Going back to section 2, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that the word "such" in the third line be struck out so that the section would read:
The expression "combine" in this act shall be deemed to have reference to combines hereinafter defined, or to combines immediately affecting trade and commerce and defined as having operated or likely to operate.
I have even great doubt of the wisdom of employing the words "likely to operate." It seems to me the only way this measure can be made effective is to couple it up with something that directly affects trade or commerce. Unless we have the power of getting rid of the Privy Council, we cannot legislate for anything outside of trade and commerce. As the section is drafted, it appears in a mere incidental form in the last clause-
-or otherwise restraining or injuring trade or commerce.
But it can hardly be necessary to set up a board for the purpose of doing the one thing, or to appoint a registrar for the purpose of
doing one thing, that the Privy Council has said we may validly do. I read from the judgment that the Dominion can call for statistical and other information which may be valuable for guidance in affecting Canada as a whole. Such information may be required before any power to regulate trade and commerce can be properly exercised. They cannot confer capacity to regulate particular trades and businesses.
Now against that vital portion of the judgment this legislation is bound to come, and when the two come in conflict, the legislation is going to fall, and not the decision of the Privy Council. I know that if I were dealing with this matter from a purely political and partisan standpoint, if we were indulging in repartee on both sides of the House, and if we were having a good election field night the discussion would be intensely more interesting, but I cannot help it. Law is a dry subject, and I cannot handle it in any other than a dry manner. Still I want the House to have the patience to follow me a little bit through the provisions of the code. Section 498 of the code says
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $4,000 and not less than $200.
And those can be increased by simple amendments.
Or to two years' imprisonment, or if a corporation, is liable to a penalty not exceeding $10,000 and not less than $1,000, who-

-agrees or arranges with any other person or with any railway, steamship, steamboat or transportation company to unduly limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing, or dealing in any article or commodity which may be a subject of trade or commerce-

-or to restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any such article or commodity, or -to unduly prevent, limit or lessen the manufacture or production of any such article or commodity or to unreasonably enhance the price thereof, or,
-to unduly prevent or lessen competition in the pro-

duction, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, transportation or supply of any such article or commodity, or in the price of insurance upon persons or property.

I want to tell the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) that I have very much enjoyed his speech, and I have no mental reservations in telling him that I particularly enjoyed that major portion of it which was devoted to a legal discussion of this question. There was one observation of his with which I might have the temerity to take issue, or at least to discuss with himself and the House. He seemed to imply that if the person laying the information in the early stages could arrive at no further point than to show that there was a state of facts, or that there were doings or circumstances which produced nothing more than the imminence of an objectionable combine there would be no offence under the act. I cannot follow the hon. gentleman there. The bill does presume a state of affairs wherein a combine is imminent; it does presuppose a state of affairs wherein a combine, may or might result from certain indicated circumstances; and it says in effect that you may nip the mischief in the bud and go on with the investigation. The very clauses read by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) from the Criminal Code went no further than that; and yet that was by his own admission a distinct crime, because those clauses read by him from the Criminal Code, I take it, relate merely to a conspiracy to do certain things. I think therefore that a state of affairs which reveals the imminence of an objectionable combine is an offence just as truly as are the cases which were cited by my hon. friend when he read from the Criminal Code itself. In the other and more elaborate phase of the hon. gentleman's very interesting and lucid legal argument, I do not presume to follow him to-night further than to say that to me it . was very interesting and I thought substantially fair. I am in hopes that this is entirely intra vires legislation. However, if it is not it will but prove another of those little knocks by which from experience we have come to understand the Act of Confederation better and better as the years roll on.
The bill has been considerably criticized on the ground that it is too easy and informal a proceeding to allow, as it does, six persons to put their heads together and submit a complaint seeking thereby an investigation. Looking at the surrounding circumstances, we must presume that the registrar will be a man of intelligence, of reasonable shrewdness and of judicial temperament. We must presume that, as a juror, he will know or can ascertain, to some substantial extent, the character of the six persons who make the complaint. It is suggested that a man might have a spite against an employer who may have dismissed him from his factory, and that for that reason he would start a merely vexatious prosecution. Well, the remedy for that lies in the common sense of the registrar. I know that in my home town we have a stipendiary magistrate, who, if someone comes and lays a charge against an alleged rum-seller, and if he detects any element of spite in the conduct of the complainant, generally gives such a man pretty short shrift in his court. So that I would take it that one who held so important an office as registrar for the Dominion under this legislation would have an opportunity of becoming fairly well acquainted with the bona fides of a complaint that was submitted to him. Further, six men are a fairly substantial number to lodge a complaint, and it is not at all probable that they would be just so many ne'er-do-wells trying to start trouble. But the registrar need not be content with a mere verbal or
