Combines-Mr. Putnam

written statement; he can at once invoke section 17 and require the complainants to go upon oath; and every layman knows that if he is reckless in a solemn affirmation or affidavit he is immediately open to the charge of perjury. Section 17a provides:
The registrar and every commissioner may accept or require evidence upon affidavit or written affirmation, in every case in which it seems to him proper-to do so.
That means that, at any stage, he may declare himself dissatisfied with the statement submitted to him and require an affidavit upon which to base the investigation. So that the mode of instituting the investigation is not quite so plain and easy and informal as many a critic in this House may imagine. The origin of an investigation is something more substantial than that; it is not nearly so intangible as many hon. members evidently suppose.
There is some misconception abroad already with regard to this bill. I find that the Ottawa Journal in an editorial has the ridiculous supposition that if the registrar produces a certificate that in his view the matter should go to the criminal court, that is all the evidence that the Attorney General will require to obtain conviction. Let me read one paragraph from the editorial. It is interesting merely as showing how wide of the mark the writer has been:
The registrar may, if he sees fit, conduct his proceedings in camera. If he signs a certificate that a combine is in existence which is detrimental to the public interest, such certificate by him is all that the prosecuting attorney need present to the court in asking for a conviction and the accused, although before the court, may be denied the right to establish or attempt to establish his innocence; the courts under this bill may become merely sentencing bodies.
This is interesting only by reason of the fact that interested parties are deluging members of parliament with propaganda; and I would suggest that if they undertake to give it the dignity of print they should be much more careful with reference to their facts. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) himself expressed an opinion entirely contrary to this only last night. His fear was that you would reveal the evidence upon which the prosecution would be based and that you would not get a conviction. He was decidedly of the view that up to the time the matter reached the criminal court nothing would have been done in the way of having a legal pronouncement made as to the guilt or innocence of the man against whom an objectionable combine was charged. He properly explained that a complete trial would have to take place in the criminal court. I am sorry the right lion, gentleman is not at this moment in his place, 
but he appeared to think that it would be a calamity if the accused were not convicted I do not look upon the matter in that light at all. It might well be that while the accused did not go over the edge of the precipice and did not actually form an objectionable combine he might have come very near the mark and that his conduct was properly a matter for investigation. We are not after blood; if it is shown that he did not go that full length, no possible harm is done. But I should say that if a responsible registrar sent the case that far it is highly probable that a man whose conduct in connection with the class of trade in which he was engaged was the subject of such suspicion, he would be pretty well warned at that stage, and the publicity would do no harm but good. Moreover, the? bill safeguards him by providing that the inquiry shall be conducted in camera if there is nothing to send up to the criminal court.
Almost every hon. member concedes that we should have laws and regulations against the miserable device of combines, trusts and mergers that are really inimical to the public interest. But hon. gentlemen opposite say: We have a criminal code that is an almost perfect remedy in itself; with a little amendment it would be a perfect remedy. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have been used to a federal statute dealing with alleged combines and mergers, apart from the criminal code, and we should continue to have such a law specially dealing with cases of that kind. Even if this is not a perfect act the deterrent effect will be of value. I say that another warning hand should be held out, in addition to what is involved in section 498, which is practically hidden away in the criminal code. Let the public know that we have made this effort; it will not interfere with legitimate or honest business. Imperfect though the bill may be, it can be improved with practice and experience at subsequent sessions of parliament. Let us make a start, because at present we practically have to fall back entirely on the criminal code.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition said, I think it was last night, that we could get so far with the procedure under this bill but no farther. I confess I could not follow him in that. He said: "You say what a combine is; you bring your evidence, but you do not tell the man complained against what he shall not do or what he shall do henceforth." Well, it seems to me that you might as well say that if at a given level crossing there were no accidents in the course of a year, you might reasonably take down the conspicuously painted sign which directed the

Combines-Mr. Lewis
attention of the public to the fact that that was a railway crossing and warned them to be careful. Or you might as well say that if in a given community nobody was prosecuted for theft during the period of a year, the provision against theft might well be struck out of the criminal code. It is only a quibble to say that the publicity of the evidence and the pronouncement of the judge for conviction or acquittal will not indicate to a reasonable merchant whose conduct has been called in question that he should adopt a certain course. It is only a quibble to say that that experience will not give him the cue as to what he shall do or what he shall not do, or as to how he shall or shall not henceforth carry on his business.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up very much time to-night; a great deal of what I had intended to say has already been said. I have listened to the various arguments for and against the proposed legislation, and I was particularly interested in the new line of argument presented by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) namely, the constitutional aspect of the question. I do not know very much about the constitutional law of Canada, but it does seem to me that colour is lent to his argument when comparison is made with the neighbouring republic to the south. There we find that there is a federal law' in regard to trusts and combines, and the great majority of the states as well have legislation dealing with the same subject. Whether or not this applies to Canada I am not in a position to say, but it does seem to me that some such legislation is needed in Canada at the present time. I do not think anyone can read the evidence that has been given before the various committees in this House without feeling that there is need for legislation such as is now proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I wish to speak not so much in regard to the spirit of the bill as to the need of it. I was particularly struck with a certain sentence uttered by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). He said that somehow or other the common people of Canada had got the idea that the high prices, the high cost of living, were due to trusts and combines.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. Is he reading from Hansard?

I quote:
I think I am right in saying that the public mind has for many years associated the high cost of living with the existence of combines, trusts and mergers ao-[DOT]called.

The hon. member used
the words "common people;" I never used that expression. I do not believe the people are common people.
The public mind, then.
Quite so.

I think the public mind
judges pretty fairly the conditions as they exist. Now, I read the bill carefully and I was heartily in support of it, but I was just a little bit disappointed when the right hon. Prime Minister, in his remarks yesterday, explained its application. It seems to me that by his explanation the bill was largely robbed of its virtue. His w'ords w'ere-I think I can quote them also exactly-that in the industrial world as we find it at the present time, combines and mergers are essential, and that there are such things as just combines and agreements. What I want to ask the House is this: What is the general reason why we have a trust? There must be some reason why business men get together to form trusts, combines and mergers. In the United States some years ago, when mergers and combines had become prevalent, an investigation was made during the course of which organizers of combines, trusts, and so on were interviewed. In almost every case it was stated by those people that the purpose of the combination was to suppress competition and to gain control. One particular sentence is significant in that connection, and I will read it. It says:
It throws off the restraint of competition by absorbing overawing or crushing out competition.
That was the reason, the investigators said, why they had combines and mergers in the United States. Now in looking over this bill and over the history of Canada it seems to me that this sentence is particularly applicable to the banking history of this country, when you consider the number of banks that have passed out of existence and the financial control that has been centered in the hands of a few men simply by absorbing and crushing out and beating out competition. In this bill I am sorry to say 1 see nothing in regard to financial combinations. It seems to me that the financial end should also be included in the bill. I can readily understand that from the standpoint of the business man competition is an evil. The chief thing that a manufacturer desires is high prices for his products. I think it is a well known economic fact and law that where combination is possible competition becomes impossible. I was speaking to one of the wholesalers in Saskatchewan only a few weeks ago, and he said that he comes down
Combines-.1/r. Lewis

east to Montreal or Toronto to buy his goods for the whole year about the 1st of May, but he said that he cannot buy them on that date. He must wait a certain time, possibly till the 15th, and then on the 15th of May he is told the price of his goods. He said that it would not make any difference to him whether he went to one man or another. There may be six firms manufacturing the same thing, but they would all have the same price. The price had already been set by the combination of these firms. So it does seem to me that where this exists, and we seem to know instinctively that such mergers and combinations do exist and set prices in Canada, such legislation as this is really needed.
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) mentioned a fact last night in regard to the tariff. I notice in the bill that one of the remedies that is proposed in section 23 is the lowering of the tariff if the price charged the consumer is too great. Now in the United States some years ago a certain man named Havemeyer uttered this sentence, "The protective tariff is the mother of trusts.'' I .do not think that statement can be swept away without some consideration. It has been said repeatedly in this House that the tariff has nothing to do with combines, mergers and such like. I believe that the tariff has something to do with them. I believe that another factor enters into it also. One is the industrial situation as we have it at the present time. We have a competitive system, and the logical outcome of any competitive system is this, that the manufacturers will endeavour to save themselves from any competition that would destroy them, and so for that reason the logical sequence of a competitive system is naturally combines and mergers for the salvation of those in the business, and until we can change our system and have some other form of co-operation it will be necessary to have combines and mergers as we have them at the present time. In the United States, with all the drastic legislation they have enacted, means have been found of outwitting the legislation and beating the anti-trust laws as they have them there.
In regard to the sentence I quoted a moment ago as to the tariff you can readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that high tariff duties charged on many articles permitted a largo measure of profit to the manufacturers with the result that there was a duplication of plants, and as a result of that duplication ruinous competition and production, and in order to escape the latter trusts were organ-

ized. Now if the tariff h*ad not granted immunity from foreign competition, people would not have ventured to place their capital in those industries. So in the first place it is a tesult of the high tariff. This artificial barrier has led to goods being manufactured in this country that never should have been produced here, and that has made it necessary for us to have combines. Where it can be materially proved that combines exist as a result of the tariff I think that section 23, if applied drastically, will have the effect of remedying the situation.
There is another thing that I feel is a great evil in regard to combines. Certain hon. members of this House have said that combines are not necessary evils. As I look over the history of combines in this country, what do I find? I find that possibly some ten, fifteen or twenty companies have been merged into one great company, and when you compare the total capitalization of ah the companies that entered into the merger with the capitalization of the merger you will find that in the new merger the capitalization is overwhelmingly above that of the sum total of the smaller companies. The result is that in a merger we get an over-capitalization. What effect has that on the consuming public? The man who is put in charge of this new merger demands that his company shall pay dividends on the over-capitalization, with the result that these mergers instead of producing a commodity at a lower price through the smaller economies that can be effected by means of a large organization, are swallowing up such benefits by paying large dividends on over-capitalized stock, with the result that the combination is of no benefit to the consumer.
Professor Jenks on behalf of the Industrial Commission in the United States refutes the thought that combines through the small economies effected bring about cheaper prices. He cites two instances, the instance of the Standard Oil Company and also the Sugar Trust. It is true that as a result of the Standard Oil Company coming into being, although that one great organization passed out of existence some years ago as far as legislation was concerned, they did lower the price, but when an investigation was made it was found that the crude oil had also been lowered in price and that the difference to the consumer was even smaller than the difference in the price which the Standard Oil had to pay for its crude oil. The same relation was also proven in regard to the sugar industry.
I view with a great deal of alarm the centralization of capital in large-scale industries

It is said that it is necessary for us to have large industries in order that we may compete successfully with other countries in other parts of the world, and yet when we look at the prices that our products sell for in foreign countries we find them very much lower than the prices in our own country. So the argument does not work out very well. It is a well known fact that in Great Britain, the United States and Canada the home consumer usually has to pay for the export trade. Large scale industries may not be an evil in themselves. They may save a great many small economies, but so far as I am concerned I believe m legislation that will be drastic enough to have complete power to investigate any merger or combine, and if it is found that it is working against the interests of the public it should be amenable to law and that the law of Canada.
I should have liked to speak in regard to the history of some of these combines and mergers in the United States. During what we might term the year of combines there we find that 149 combinations were formed in which the subscribed capital amounted to over three billions of dollars, a menace practically to the public. It was the fear of destructive elements of competition that forced these people to combine. I ask the government, could this have taken place in the United States or in Canada if free trade had prevailed? As a result of combination in the United States the Standard Oil Company paid 12 per cent in dividends in 1891 and in 1902 no less than 45 per cent. Yet to all appearances, they give some semblance of competition to the people of the United States. As far as possible the authorities have endeavoured in the United States to overcome these combinations. I understand that in 1892 the Supreme Court of New York state declared that the organization of the Standard Trust Company was illegal. What did the company do? Immediately following the declaration they adopted a new plan. They divided up the shares, but continued to hold the great majority of them just as completely as in the case of the old Trust Company. That is the danger in regard to any legislation that we put upon the statute books.
The spirit of the measure that we are now called upon to pass is all right. It is a step, and a good step, in the right direction; but I would like to see the responsibility for taking action placed not upon any six individuals, but upon the government. The rights of the people are in question here. They are bearing a heavy burden at the
8, 1923	.
Combines-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
present time, as we find out from the evidence given before investigating parliamentary committees; and it seems to me that the government should not only enact this legislation but follow it up by such action as will free the people from the operations of these unjust mergers and combines. Combinations may be necessary in the industrial life of the country but when they operate unjustly the people should be given a chance to escape from the extortionate cnarges which these combines often exact instead of remaining satisfied with legitimate profits.

I do not intend to offer any very extended remarks at this late hour, but believing this to be the most important legislation that has come before the House this session I wish to put myself on record as being strong'y in its favour. During the past few years the subject with which this bill deals has been a very live one throughout the Dominion, and has been discussed pro and con from every platform. Now we believe the time has arrived when some relief should be given the public along the line indicated.
The criticisms which have been directed against the measure to-night are not very well founded in my opinion. Y e must make a start somewhere. Legal questions will always be raised in connection with any proposed legislation; gentlemen of the legal profession will always discover points for discussion no matter what the provisions of a bill may be.
I believe this is a start in the right direction. We do not want any better evidence of that than the sensation which it has created throughout the country. Hon. members have been receiving letters and circulars from combines and trusts showing they have awakened to the situation which confronts them and realize there is going to be something doing in the future. I cannot altogether follow the argument of some hon. members who maintain that in a free trade country there will be no combines. Personally, I am strongly in favour of a policy of free trade and I would like the time to come when we, in the lower provinces at least, might enjoy that great boon. But the existence of free trade is no deterrent against the formation of combines and trusts. We read in the public journals that in the case of articles upon which there is a low rate of duty combinations have been formed on both sides of the international boundary for the purpose of getting together and holding up prices. So that I am not able to follow the reasoning of hon. gentlemen who argue that combines will not exist where free trade obtains.
Combines-Mr. COMMONS
Mackenzie King
I was pleased to hear the remarks of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) this afternoon. He sounded a splendid note in his address and I believe his remarks will have their due effect on some of the combines to which he referred, notably the sugar trust. We know, also, that the manufacturers on a large scale of hats, caps, boots and shoes are seemingly making exorbitant profits. If this bill is brought into operation and one or two of the offenders taught a severe lesson I believe it will tend to put an end to this unjust system and that in future those who conduct industrial enterprises will be satisfied with a more reasonable margin of profit. I do not think anyone in this House wishes to crowd any manufacturer out of business. What we do desire is that he shall be satisfied with a fair profit and not exact exorbitant rates from the consuming public.
I am strongly in favour of this legislation and am proud to belong to the party responsible for introducing it. I am only too glad to follow a Prime Minister who has brought such a bill as this before parliament; it is one that should receive the support of every hon. member. Let us adopt this measure and show the country that we are behind the Prime Minister and intend to see that it is put into force. I do not take much stock in the argument that this bill is not workrl le. As I say, this legislation is a start in the right direction and if experience discloses any imperfections the law can be amended from time to time. Let us all unite in passing this bill and show the country that we mean business.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If any hon.
member desires to speak he should take advantage of the present opportunity before the mover of the resolution closes the debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The discussion which has continued now for the greater part of two days has disclosed, as has already been alluded to by one hon. member opposite, that the House is practically unanimously agreed that in this age of competition it is unavoidable that there should be large combinations of capital and business interests. It was pretty generally admitted, with the exception of possibly one speaker, that industrial combinations in one form or another were inevitable having regard to world competition as it exists to-day. This legislation starts out from the point of view that such is the case. The hon. member to whom I have referred, also mentioned that new times bring new dei elopments and new methods of dealing with new situations. I think it is worthy of note in that connection that from the point of view of

legislation on matters of this kind a real advance has been made. The Canadian parliament in 1909 was virtually the first parliament to take the attitude that it was not proper to legislate against combinations as such, but rather that it was from the point of view of guarding against the ill effects of large combination that legislation of this kind should proceed. It has now become pretty generally accepted that that is the correct point of view to adopt.
Let me refer by way of example to the Sherman Anti-Trust legislation of the United States, regarded at the time as the best possible method of proceeding. It started from the point of view that combinations as such were wrong, and that combinations of large business interests were an evil. It was found, as endeavours were made to enforce that law, that its enforcement was an impossibility: that it was really proceeding from a wrong point of view. To-day we find that members on both sides of the House are in general agreement as to the right of combination where it is legitimately carried on. This would have been impossible fifteen years ago. We may feel in the circumstance that the world has moved a step forward in an understanding of the problems of modern business.
Another point on which the House has been m agreement is that combinations which operate against the public interest or are detrimental to the public interest should not be supported or permitted. Well if we are in agreement on both these points, I fail to see wherein any reasonable objection can be urged to the legislation which is being presented to parliament to-night. It is based on the supposition that combinations will continue to exist; and if properly conducted have a right to exist. The only kind of combination which it pretends in any way adversely to affect is a combination carried to the point where the public interest suffers in order that private interests may make gains to which they are rightly entitled. If the country will appreciate, and the House will appreciate that such is the sole purpose of the legislation, the bringing to time, so to speak, combinations that in their secret business methods go beyond what is reasonable and fair, to prevent what amounts to extortion as regards the public, and that this is all that is being aimed at in this legislation, there should, I think, be unanimity of expression in favour of some legislation of the kind.
Let me say a word about the relations of the public to big business. I have heard a great deal in th's debate about the business interests and the rights of business, and the

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
non-interference with private rights and the like. I think it is sometimes forgotten that perhaps, after all, the public is one of the parties to industry just as much as any of the other parties. It was assumed at one time that all the problems of industry were problems that related solely to labour and capital. Then there came forward another class that claimed the right to be considered in the discussion of these problems. That was the class that describes itself as management, those possessing managerial ability. It was pointed out that while capital could do a great deal, and labour could do a great deal, unless the two vTere in some way brought together and directed intelligently under the skill, the business ability of a guiding genius very little could be accomplished in the way of large business. It is now admitted that these three groups are entitled to consideration in matters pertaining to industry but a fourth group of late has come more and more to the fore, and is beginning to receive more and more its due consideration,, I mean the public; the public which, for a long time, was ignored altogether. Labour, capital and managerial ability each claimed its share of consideration in the distribution of the fruits of industry, but the public was left to shift for itself. So. far as this legislation is concerned, it is brought forward in the name of that fourth party, in the name of the public without whom neither labour nor capital nor managerial ability could accomplish or achieve anything.
It may be asked, Mr. Speaker, how it is that large businesses are able to expand and to carry on to the extent they do? It is in virtue of what the public does, or permits to be done, through its organization in one form or another. Were it not for law and order as preserved by the public through governments what could large businesses achieve? Were it not for what the public permits in the way of organization of transportation, organized banking and credit facilities, agencies of communication and the like, what could large business achieve one way or the other? Were it not for what the public does in furthering education, encouraging invention, stimulating trade through its consular representatives, through its trade agencies and the like, were it not for what is achieved by diplomatic representatives, where would large business be in its successful ventures throughout the world? I might go on and mention the very direct aids that are given to big business in such matters as have been referred to frequently in this debate, as for example the tariff, bounties and other
forms of special protection given to large business. By whom? By the public, through the agency of its representatives in parliament. Well, if it is true that the public is rendering this service to industry, surely the public has a right to demand of industry and business that, so far as it is concerned, it will be protected from any extreme and extortionate act on the part of large business through the facilities it affords. That is all the government is asking for in this bill.
We come in the name of the fourth party to industry, we come in the name of the public, the people at large, and say to large business interests, whether it be manufacturing, wholesale or retail businesses, agencies of communication, commercial enterprises or the like, but for what the people do, not merely in creating demands for commodities of these industries and arranging for their distribution, but in the other ways to which I have referred, large business would not have any place in the community at all. We say, in consequence of that, the public is entitled to know where it stands in reference to its part and relation to industry as a whole.
A great discussion over this measure has had special reference to the criminal offence which is created in this enactment. Hon. members opposite, and particularly my hon. friend for St. John (Mr. Baxter) have spoken more especially in reference to the criminal section of this bill. I would like for the moment to have hon. members forget that there is a criminal section in the bill, or a criminal offence intended to be created by the legislation. As I explained briefly, both at the time of introducing the measure and on moving the second reading, the law falls broadly into two phases. The first has to do with investigations, and the second has to do with criminal prosecutions. Let us for the moment leave to one side altogether the possible intra vires of the legislation, so far as the criminal prosecution is concerned, and consider the other aspect of the legislation, that namely which has to do with investigation. So far as I am concerned, in my own view of it, I would say that the powers of investigation given under the act are likely to be more effective in achieving the end aimed at than the new criminal offence which the bill creates. I think powers of investigation, rightly, legitimately and carefully exercised will go far towards curing ills, with respect to which penalties would be found wholly ineffective. In other words, as I expressed it the other day, there are certain classes of offences, those particularly which relate to social and economic conditions.

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
which publicity is infinitely more effective to prevent and to redress than penalty. Once the public has the facts before it, once it has the necessary information, has got at the truth, once the situation is known from within, and that it affects the public adversely, the public may be expected to find some means, through its parliament and in other ways, to provide the necessary remedy or cure for any particular situation. That is the point of view from which this legislation proceeds. It seeks to frame machinery through the agency of which the light of day can be let into transactions with a view of disclosing whether these transactions are in the public interest or against it. In other words, it seeks to do for the social system in the matter of its moral health what the light of day or the sun does for the physical body in the matter of its health. Exclude the sun and its power from the physical universe, and very soon you find disease setting in where there should be health and vigour. Prevent the light of day from penetrating the secret recesses of various business devices, and very soon industry, instead of being the great servant of humanity which it should be, comes to be an instrument to be used against the well-being of the people themselves.
This legislation, in providing for investigation, does so, as I have said, for the purpose of bringing out the facts, bringing out information. My right hon. friend said that the measure was of no value, because it meant simply one investigation after another. At this point, may I draw attention to the character of the criticism which has proceeded from hon. gentlemen opposite? The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) was the first to speak at great length on this legislation, his whole attack was that it went too far; that it was vexatious; that it was altogether harassing and extreme, and that it would be an injury to private business. The leader of the Opposition went to the other extreme-
I said the same thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the right hon. member said the same thing, and he also said something directly the opposite.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. He generally takes both sides at the same time. He said that the legislation had no teeth in it.

Hear, hear.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING. I think he remembers that. On the one hand it was exfMr. Mackenzie King.]
treme in one direction, and on the other it was extreme in the other direction.
Legislation can be very vexatious without having teeth in it. That can be done by the effect of its claws.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If we have succeeded in bringing into this House legislation which to one section of our opponents opposite appears to be altogether short of the mark, and to another section appears to go much too far in the other direction, that is pretty good evidence that we have struck the happy medium by avoiding extremes. That is exactly what we have sought to do. As to the investigation having no advantages, might I ask my right hon. friend, when he says investigation is powerless to be of any service, how is it that we have royal commissions appointed to inquire into problems with respect to which light is needed? Why is it, might I ask, that we have committees of parliament at the present time trying to get at the truth in regard to many important matters? Is it not a faot that both royal commissions and committees of parliament sitting at this very time are recognized by all hon. members as rendering the kind of service that is essential for legislation along right and proper lines, and for adequately informing public opinion? Is that not the best answer to anything that can be said against investigations into combines, monopolies, trusts or mergers which may tend to operate against the public interest? If the facts can be ascertained, a remedy will very soon be found.

The right hon. member puts that as a question to me. I do not say that investigation is useless; but I say that a permanent body for purely investigational purposes without power to enforce its finding, is a surplusage. The power of investigation, in any individual instance or contingency the government has without this legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not a permanent body that this particular legislation undertakes to create.
The registrar?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The registrar
is one individual; he is not a permanent body in the sense in which that term is generally used. The effective investigations will be by the different commissioners who will be appointed to deal with cases which the registrar thinks are deserving of more careful investigation. My right hon. friend says that because there is no power to enforce the finding of the particular commissioner, the investigation is, therefore, of no value. To argue

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
in that way is to deny any value to public opinion, to deny all value to the power of parliament, and those are the two greatest powers which the people have in the matter of self-protection. The power of a well-informed public opinion and the power of parliament to deal with any situation of which it may have accurate and concrete knowledge

that is the power which this legislation brings into being. It provides the machinery whereby, in regard to matters which directly affect the people, which affect them vitally as regards their food, clothing, housing and all the things which go to make up the necessities of their existence, they may get accurate information; this it does in order that the framers of public opinion throughout the country, whether they be in parliament, on the platform, of the press or in whatever form public opinion cares to express itself, may have an opportunity to help to redress a public wrong. I ask hon. members if that is not the greatest power which it is possible to give. What is the power
10 p.m. of the criminal code to prosecute some particular person or group of persons in comparison with the power of spreading broadcast throughout the land accurate and true information with regard to a situation which is inimical to the public interest, and which the people themselves are certain to be concerned in remedying. Take it as respects legislation. How is parliament to know what is the best course to take in the matter of legislation unless it gets true and accurate information? If you wait until the criminal code is put into operation against some particular concern, you may never hear of the evil. An important inquiry has been going on respecting freight rates on the Great Lakes. I imagine the country has become pretty well aware at the present moment of how necessary that inquiry has been. I wonder if that inquiry would ever have taken place under the criminal code if there had been no investigation. Investigation where properly conducted is the one thing which will bring to the attention of parliament what is necessary in the way of legislation to protect the public interest. Therefore, if this legislation went no further than simply to provide what it does in the way of machinery for investigation, it would be rendering a great and much needed public service.
But there are other immediate methods of action which follow upon investigation, apart altogether from the criminal procedure. Under this legislation the Governor in Council with respect to an article of commerce which is shewn to be unduly enhanced in price as a consequence of the tariff, has power immediately to reduce the duty or to wipe out the duty altogether. That is apart from any criminal offence created in the measure. That is a power given to the government itself to be exercised at any and at all times.
May I draw this further fact to the attention of the House? The value of a measure of this kind is not to be estimated by the number of prosecutions that take place, nor by the number of investigations. Rather is it to be estimated by the power of prevention which lies in the fact that it is known that a certain course of procedure will inevitably lead to an investigation and disclosure of conduct that is contrary to the public interest. Is it not desirable to have upon the statute books of this country a power of that kind which stands at all times as a safeguard of the interest of the public?
As regards big business itself, I think it is rendering big business the greatest possible service that such a power should at any and at all times be found on our statutes. There are members of this House who view with alarm at times the advance of what they refer to as socialism, the tendency for the state itself to take over control in a variety of directions. What is it that more than anything else has been responsible for the advance which socialism has made? It has been the feeling in the minds of the masses of the people that, in some way or another, their interests are not being protected or looked after; that in some way a power other than themselves is greater than the power of the state itself. You help to remove a feeling of that kind when you put it into the hands of any six persons, who have reason to think there is some social injustice under which they are suffering, to have that matter investigated and to have their minds set right as to whether or not the facts which they believe, are true.
A reference has been made to the old Combines Investigation Act of 1910, under which it has been stated, there were only one or two prosecutions. I had a little to do with the administration of that act, and I know that as respects a number of industries in connection with which people believed or were asserting that some injustice was being worked, once these people had it within their power to bring about an investigation, they refrained altogether from taking action because they were unable to submit even a prima facie case sufficient to establish ground for an investigation of the charges they had so freely made. I believe it will be so in the case of this legislation. I believe that men who get up and, without any justification for their words, begin to attack large business

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
simply because it is large, once they are given an opportunity to make good the charges which they are ready to bring against such business will be more careful about the use of their words and directing accusations against big concerns. From that point of view I think the legislation is calculated to be of service to large business as well as to the public itself.
Now I may touch upon one or two other points that have been referred to. But first of all let me say that if at the time of introducing the legislation, I had had any doubts about the wisdom of it, those doubts have been completely removed through the endeavours that have been made, in the name of so-called private business interests to prevent any investigation whatever. What has legitimate business to fear from the light of day? Why should men be afraid that the power of investigation is going to lead to all kinds of serious trouble, if there is nothing to conceal? I think that there must be plenty of work to be done under legislation of this kind if some of the fears which appear to be entertained by some gentlemen are real. So far as anything is reasonable or fair or just in business relations it will not be affected by this legislation; but if there are existent, in connection with business, practices which will not stand the light of day, then probably there is justification for some of the alarm and some of the fear that has been expressed as a possible consequence of investigation. That however is only a reason why this parliament, which is here to protect the interests of the people as a whole, should Bee to it that legislation such as that being con-considered, is placed upon the statutes.
Now, it has been asserted that many of the methods which large industry adopts in price fixing and in other forms of combination and agreement are wholly in the public interest.
I admit that; I have so stated; and I am willing to agree with anyone who points out that by large combination and price fixing you may help to bring about in industry a stability which otherwise it might not possess, as well as economies and increased efficiency. That is all perfectly true. But it is also true that by these very same methods men who are not actuated by a public spirit, but who think primarily of all that it is possible for them to exact from the public, may carry their price fixing and their agreements to the point of monopoly in a manner which will be detrimental to the public interest; and as soon as private rights reach the point where they become public wrongs, at that moment it

seems to me there has been a departure from what is just and fair and the commission of a wrong that to all intents and purposes is a crime. When you get a public wrong that affects the people as a whole then surely the government of the country is entitled to make a criminal offence out of that which is against the interests of the public. That is all that this legislation seeks to do. It makes no>
criminal offence until it has been established, by the most careful and conservative processes conceivable that there is reason to believe that the public in some way has suffered an injustice from certain conditions complained of. Take the steps leading up to the creation of a criminal offence. I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) who said that this legislation tended to erect a crime out of what was common sense. That was his way of stating the criminal aspect of the bill. Well, at what point does the legislation erect a crime out of common sense, as the hon. gentleman says? In the first place, at least six persons who are British subjects must present to the registrar, who will be appointed by the government, which will be responsible to parliament for the kind of appointment it makes, sufficient ground for him to believe that there exists a combination which is operating to the detriment of the public and against its interest. The registrar is given power to call before him the parties concerned, to go to their place of business if he so desires and thinks it necessary, and to gather information from various sources, with a view to ascertaining whether there is really sufficient ground to believe that the business is not being conducted in accordance with legitimate and accepted methods but is going beyond that to the injury of the people at large. Unless the registrar is satisfied that such is the case, there is no further investigation of the particular combination of which complaint has been made. If the registrar, after having examined the case carefully, comes to the conclusion that the men who have presented their complaint are not cranks nor disgruntled, dismissed employees, nor any of like classes to which reference has been made, but that they are sober, sensible citizens who have a regard for the well-being of the public at large,-if in short he comes to the conclusion that there are just reasons for believing that a combination is operating to the detriment of the people, then he reports to the minister, who thereupon asks 'the Govemor-in-Council to appoint a commissioner to make a larger and more careful inquiry. Now, the government is responsible for the commissioner that will.

Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
be appointed; no government is likely to appoint at random any kind of an individual to that position. The government will be responsible to parliament for the class of men it appoints to discharge this responsible duty. The worth of any finding that will be made by a commissioner will depend on the class of man chosen for the particular position; and unless the commissioner, after having made a full inquiry, after having given all the parties concerned the fullest opportunity of making out their case, is convinced that the action of the combine is against the public interest, nothing further comes of the matter; nothing at all by way of prosecution. But that is not all. Even after the commissioner has presented his report, which parliament will be in a position to call for at any time, it then remains for the attorney general of a province or the Solicitor General of the Dominion to enter prosecution against the combine concerned. The question is, will an attorney general of a province or the Solicitor General of the Dominion enter a prosecution against some concern with respect to which the evidence is not strong enough in his opinion to effect a conviction? Up to that point there is possible nothing in the nature of a criminal prosecution against any concern which is alleged to be injuring the public interest. Yet my hon. friend says that the legislation seeks to erect a crime out of what is common sense. I think that if we have regard to the different stages that have to be passed before we reach the criminal stage we shall agree that by the time we get to that point it is high time that some legislation should "erect" a crime out of a course of behaviour that would lead that number of different persons, looking at all sides of the case, to the belief that the public is suffering a wrong by reason of a certain course of conduct. So much, then, for the criminal offence which the act creates.
But my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition and those associated with him have said to us over and over again, "Why not rely on the Criminal Code? You have everything in the Criminal Code which you want. Why add any other legislation?" Well, may I ask my hon. friend, why did he not, when in office, rely upon the Criminal Code, if it was sufficient? Why did he introduce the Combines and Fair Prices Act or the Board of Commerce Act if the Criminal Code was sufficient for all purposes?
I told my hon. friend that when I spoke.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What was the answer?

I stated that in those days there was very great business activity and that very large profits were being made. It is all right to erect a Board of Commerce; there is some result in it if you give that board power to give effect to its findings. I stated to the Prime Minister that if he thought similar conditions existed now he might go ahead, but that he should give his board power to give effect to its findings, and that until he did that his legislation was a sham.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This afternoon, my right hon. friend's associate,-the hon.member for South York (Mr. Maclean), said, I think, that he believed that to-day very large profits were being made, that to-day business was being conducted very much as it had been when my right hon. friend was in office. If that is the case, there was just as much need for the Criminal Code when he was in office as there is to-day, and the Criminal Code ought to have been just as effective then as it is now.
It was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
But my right hon. friend did not rely on the Criminal Code; he introduced the Combines and Fair Prices Act and he introduced the Board of Commerce Act. I am not complaining of his action; I think he did what was right, except in restricting actions under the code. I think he was right in believing that the Criminal Code of itself was really of very little use.
It is a fact, and no one knows it better than my right hon. friend, that in regard to the class of subjects which we have been discussing to-day, the criminal law is in a very different position from that which obtains when we are dealing with the class of criminal cases to which we are most accustomed. In cases of theft, murder, perjury, any of these crimes, there is little or no difficulty in ascertaining that a certain wrong has been done; the difficulty is to apprehend the wrong-doer and bring him to justice. As regards the average subject with which the criminal law deals the offence itself is apparent on the surface, but it is not so in respect to most of the evils that arise out of the methods resorted to by combinations in restraint of trade. As a rule these are framed with the assistance of the best legal advice that can be obtained; they are worked out in the most careful manner. The men who have to ao with the administering of questionable methods of proceeding in business usually take all possible precautions to see that there is as little publicity as possible with respect to what is being



Combines-Mr. Mackenzie King
done. In such cases the difficulty is to discover and bring to light the evil of which complaint is made, but when it is discovered, when the facts are brought to light, then the Criminal Code may well become effective. That is the basis on which . this legislation proceeds. It seeks by the agency of investigation to briDg to light methods which will not stand the light of day, if there be any such. And when they are brought to light, then, with the evidence assembled, the bill provides a means whereby that evidence may, at the instance of the Attorney Geneial or of the Solicitor General, be used for the purpose of bringing the combine into court and obtaining such redress as may be possible by means of a criminal prosecution.
Mention has been made of au alleged inquisitorial phase of the legislation I think the member from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said that because this investigation was to be carried on in private before the registrar or before the commissioners, it, was in the nature of a star chamber proceeding. Well, so far as I am concerned I am perfectly willing to have that investigation as open as the day, both before the registrar and before the commissioners, and if my hon. friend will move an amendment to that effect, I shall be willing to abide by what the House says in regard to it. The reason that the investigation has been made private is because the so-called interests, those that have made their representations, have expressed it as their opinion that.it should be in private.
Perhaps the public think otherwise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The public may think otherwise, but I think the interests are right in the point of view which they present, for this reason; the investigation may be made at the instance of any six persons, and I do not think it is desirable, if it can be avoided, to have the affairs of any business brought out before the public to any greater extent than may be necessary, until it is shown that the course of procedure complained of is really contrary to the public interest. That is the nature of the protection which this legislation gives to legitimate business. It seeks to prevent any undue publicity; but if and when it is shown before the registrar or before the commissioners that the method of procedure of the combine in question is contrary to the public interest, then the veil of privacy which for the time being has been thrown about what has been assumed to be a legitimate business is withdrawn; the evidence may then be made public. The particular

combine, if it has been operating against the public interest, no longer gets any protection in the way of privacy; on the contrary, the public at large are given all the information that has been secured. I think that is perhaps the best way of proceeding.
My right hon. friend says that what we have in this legislation exists in large part in other legislation. He referred to the provisions of the Customs Act which give to the Governor in Council power to reduce the tariff after an inquiry by a judge, and he referred also to certain powers given under the Patent Act for the revocation of patent rights. Well, that legislation was in existence when the Combines Act of 1909 came into effect. It was thought advisable to make it clear in that act just what the different classes of remedies were to which the public might look when there was evidence adduced that the public interest was suffering through combines in restraint of trade. That legislation existed exactly in the form in which it exists to-day, when my right hon. friend introduced his Combines and Fair Prices Act and his Board of Commerce Act; and he embodied both the clauses-the very clauses that we have here- in that legislation.

Certainly-if the right hon. gentleman will permit me. I do not find fault with putting them in. But we have these clauses in other statutes and there is no need of a new bill merely to enact them twice. What I say is that my right hon. friend, while he is having his legislation, may just as well have all the remedies in one bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Now my right hon. friend is coming to my point of view. That is precisely what the government seeks to do; it is seeking to assemble in one piece of legislation all that is relevant to the particular subject under consideration. By bringing together the different parts of existing legislation that have a direct relation to the investigation and prosecution of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, in whatever form these pieces of legislation may appear, we have perhaps taken the most effective means of preventing combines of one kind or another from proceeding contrary to the public interest.
As to the constitutional aspect of the question. to which the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) has referred, I think the House may well accept, for the time being at all events, the opinion of the Department of Justice that what we are doing in this legislation is entirely intra vires of this parliament. However, if it is not, I would still think it was

Combines-Division
advisable to introduce this legislation at the present session rather than to wait a little longer. The sooner we find out how far we can legislate in this matter the better, and I would say to my right hon. friend that if at any time it should appear that this legislation in any particular is not intra vires of this parliament, and that by expanding the Criminal Code or adding to it in any way we can still deal effectively with the evil we are seeking to remedy, if the present government should remain in office and be there in office, very little time would be lost in making the Criminal Code all that he or any other member of the House may desire in that regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext: This item is to provide for the examination and certification of masters and mates of ships. The law requires them to have certificates. There are three districts in which examinations are held, the eastern divison, the Great Lakes division and the western division. The expenditure last year was $19,958.29. It will be about the same this year.
Who conducts the examination?

The department has a certain number of officers in every district. In my hon. friend's district we have Captain Charles Eddy, who is the supervising examiner at Vancouver, Captain Davis at Victoria, and Captain Lindsay at Nelson.
Are these examinations held once a year?

No, only when candidates offer themselves for examination. In Vancouver there were twenty-three masters examined last year and given certificates, thir-

teen mates and five second mates; and in the same proportion in other places in the western division.

SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS. JOINT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER MATTERS OF COMMON INTEREST
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received a message from the Senate requesting the House of Commons to unite with the Senate in the appointment of a joint committee to be composed of an equal number of members, not exceeding five, of each House to consider the following matters:
1.	The forms of bills and the best means of affording information and assistance in the consideration thereof at all stages of legislation in both Houses of parliament.
2.	The better distribution of the work of legislation between the two Houses.
3.	The practical operation of the provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act, R.S.C., 1906. chapter 10, respecting the attendance of Senators and members of the House of Commons and the expediency of making any alterations in these provisions;
And that the hon. Messieurs Beique, Belcourt, Calder, Green and Pardee have been appointed to act on behalf of the Senate as members of said joint committee.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
